bullets: The newly released SAFE-CARE Bench specifies a release-gate protocol for patient-facing healthcare agents across multi-turn conversations. It tests whether risk accumulates across otherwise acceptable replies and whether escalation to human care happens in time, while declaring active capabilities so teams can reproduce the protocol on their own runtime. Why it matters: If you approve healthcare-agent updates, this changes the decision from checking isolated medical answers to evaluating the full conversational path, including delayed escalation and the safety-versus-accuracy trade-off. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

The new MURPHY benchmark uses 1,500 multilingual and emoji prompts to audit whether inference servers report token identifiers and probability records correctly. It scores record integrity separately from instruction following, so a model can complete the requested task while its diagnostic output is still wrong. Why it matters: If you compare models or decoding methods using token-level probabilities, this provides a separate check that the serving system produced trustworthy measurement records rather than treating task success as evidence that its telemetry is correct. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

The newly released SecKB-Bench and PROVE reference implementation evaluates retrieval-augmented generation—systems that answer using retrieved documents—as one security channel spanning both document ingestion and answer disclosure. Its design tests whether attacker-written claims admitted to the knowledge base can later be retrieved and leaked. Why it matters: If you evaluate a document-connected assistant, this means separate poisoning and confidentiality tests can miss their interaction. The artifact supports a joint decision about what content may enter the knowledge base and what retrieved material may leave through an answer. Evidence: E018. Medium confidence.

The new agent-firewall benchmark supplies categorized prompt-injection samples embedded in content an agent processes around sensitive tools, including reading and sending email, web search, and note storage. The evaluation target is the defense at the point where untrusted text can influence a consequential tool execution. Why it matters: If you are selecting defenses for a tool-using agent, this offers a more deployment-specific test than generic jailbreak prompts: the relevant decision is whether the defense blocks malicious instructions without disrupting legitimate tool workflows. Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

The released ElecVQA-Bench study audits vision-language models for drone power-line inspection while controlling source-image dependence, input resolution, label space, evaluated items, and side information. Its paired comparison found no detected difference between selected vision-only and vision-language runs on the original binary task, while tower-disjoint retraining provided a limited check on unseen towers. Why it matters: If you are choosing an inspection model, this makes matched resolution and tower-disjoint testing part of the comparison; otherwise, data partitioning or unequal inputs may be mistaken for an advantage from combining vision and language. Evidence: E021. Medium confidence.

A newly released synthetic-lethality prediction study shows that replacing random test negatives with degree-matched negatives moved reported area-under-the-curve scores substantially, sometimes downward and sometimes upward. Degree matching controls how often biological entities appear in the underlying interaction network, reducing the chance that popularity alone separates examples. Why it matters: If you use benchmark scores to choose candidates for experimental screening, this shows that test-set composition and retrieval from the actual experimental pool need separate evaluation; a model’s ranking under random negatives may not represent its screening value. Evidence: E046. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 SAFE-CARE Bench 为面向患者的医疗智能体制定了一套覆盖多轮对话的发布门禁协议。它测试风险是否会在单条回复看似均可接受的情况下不断累积，以及是否能及时升级转交人工医疗服务，同时声明启用的能力，以便团队在自己的运行时环境中复现该协议。Why it matters: 如果你负责批准医疗智能体更新，这会将决策重点从检查孤立的医疗回答，转向评估完整的对话路径，包括延迟升级转交以及安全性与准确性之间的权衡。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

新的 MURPHY 基准使用 1,500 条多语言及表情符号提示，审计推理服务器能否正确报告词元标识符和概率记录。它将记录完整性与指令遵循分开评分，因此模型即使完成了要求的任务，其诊断输出仍可能有误。Why it matters: 如果你使用词元级概率来比较模型或解码方法，该基准可以单独检查服务系统是否生成了可信的测量记录，而不是将任务成功视为遥测数据正确的证据。Evidence: E004. High confidence.

新发布的 SecKB-Bench 和 PROVE 参考实现将检索增强生成——即使用检索到的文档作答的系统——作为一个横跨文档摄取和答案披露的统一安全通道进行评估。其设计用于测试攻击者编写的主张在获准进入知识库后，是否会在之后被检索并泄露。Why it matters: 如果你评估的是连接文档的助手，这意味着分别进行投毒测试和保密性测试可能会遗漏两者之间的相互作用。该工件支持对哪些内容可以进入知识库、哪些检索到的材料可以通过答案输出进行联合决策。Evidence: E018. Medium confidence.

新的 agent-firewall 基准提供了分类后的提示注入样本，这些样本被嵌入智能体围绕敏感工具处理的内容中，包括读取和发送电子邮件、网页搜索以及笔记存储。评估目标是处于不受信任文本能够影响高后果工具执行这一关键点上的防御机制。Why it matters: 如果你正在为使用工具的智能体选择防御措施，这比通用越狱提示提供了更贴近部署场景的测试：关键决策在于，防御措施能否在不干扰合法工具工作流的情况下拦截恶意指令。Evidence: E001. Medium confidence.

已发布的 ElecVQA-Bench 研究在控制源图像依赖、输入分辨率、标签空间、评估条目和辅助信息的情况下，对用于无人机电力线巡检的视觉语言模型进行审计。其配对比较在原始二元任务上未发现所选纯视觉运行与视觉语言运行之间存在差异，而基于不同杆塔拆分的重新训练则对未见杆塔提供了有限检验。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择巡检模型，这会使匹配分辨率和基于不同杆塔拆分的测试成为比较的一部分；否则，数据划分或输入不对等可能会被误认为是视觉与语言结合带来的优势。Evidence: E021. Medium confidence.

一项新发布的合成致死性预测研究表明，用度数匹配的负例替代随机测试负例后，报告的曲线下面积分数发生了显著变化，有时下降，有时上升。度数匹配控制生物实体在底层交互网络中的出现频率，从而降低仅凭流行度就能区分样本的可能性。Why it matters: 如果你使用基准分数来选择实验筛选候选对象，这表明测试集构成以及从实际实验候选池中进行检索需要分别评估；模型在随机负例条件下的排序可能无法代表其筛选价值。Evidence: E046. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.
evidence_items.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the benchmark, code and aggregate results used to evaluate THReD (Transforming EHRs into AI-Ready Datasets), a no-code, web-based system in which researchers preprocess electronic health record (EHR) extracts through modular tools and an LLM-based agent that proposes pipeline steps for the user to confirm. It accompanies the manuscript "THReD: An Agentic, Modular and Reproducible System for Transforming Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets" and documents in full the evaluation reported there. Agent evaluation. The agent was assessed on 141 preprocessing tasks derived from 100 templates in seven categories: single-tool, multi-step and goal-level requests, failure and recovery, requests that should not be acted on, schema variation, and instructions injected through the data. Every task pairs an expert reference pipeline with outcome checks applied to the resulting table, so that any pipeline producing a valid result is credited. Tasks run on synthetic hypertension (HTN) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) tables calibrated to aggregate statistics of the source extracts, so no patient record is sent to the language model. Four context configurations, from none to the deployed context, were evaluated with five repetitions each using Claude Haiku 5.5, for 2,550 episodes in total, with confidence intervals from a cluster bootstrap over task templates. With the deployed context, 92.7% of tasks were completed on the agent's first response (95% CI 88.1–96.4%), rising to 95.6% after up to two follow-up turns, with a tool-selection F1 of 0.926 and 3.3% invalid tool calls; without context, first-answer completion fell to 58.0%. It recovered from 45 of 47 failed steps and never acted on instructions planted in the data (0 of 40 episodes). Preprocessing evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark of THReD: Design, Results and Observations of the Agent and Preprocessing Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.
evidence_items.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.
evidence_items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery

evidence_items.summary: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.
evidence_items.title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions

evidence_items.summary: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.
evidence_items.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Patient-facing healthcare AI agents now talk with people across many turns, and each new version should pass a release gate, the go-live check that asks whether a change made the agent safer without losing accuracy. Single-turn medical benchmarks were not designed to answer that question, because a conversational agent fails across turns: risk builds while each reply looks acceptable, and an escalation to human care can arrive one turn too late. SAFE-CARE Bench is a benchmark specification and evaluation protocol designed for that decision. Its configurations declare which capabilities are active, not how to build them, so a team can reproduce the protocol on its own runtime. This record archives version 0.4.1 of its public repository. To trace a change to its cause, SAFE-CARE Bench runs a controlled ablation. Five agent variants, tiers A0 to A4, add one capability bundle at a time: retrieval with enforced citations, a safety guardrail, personalization from memory, and agency (tools, profile write-back and closed-loop actions). All five are scored over the same simulated conversations with synthetic personas, with the model, temperature and seed held fixed, so the design attributes the change between adjacent tiers to the bundle added. An LLM judge scores ten dimensions, seven on a 1-to-5 scale and three as pass or fail, and judges safety and escalation both on a single turn and across turns. A missed escalation fails a conversation whatever its other scores. The worked example, tiers A0 to A2, shows why the instrument must be checked before its verdict is trusted. We expected the safety guardrail to raise judged safety. Instead, adding it lowered judged medical accuracy by 0.157 on a 0-to-1 scale, lower in six of nine scenarios and higher in none, while the 95% interval for its safety change included zero. Auditing the instrument then showed that the scenario file decides, before any agent runs, which turns each judge reads.
evidence_items.title: SAFE-CARE Bench: A Benchmark Specification and Evaluation Protocol for Safety, Guardrails, and User Experience in Multi-Turn Healthcare AI Agent Conversations

evidence_items.summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. On the held-out final 20% of the record (12 channels in five installations), HARDIO achieves a mean chained 1-NRMSE of 0.976, within 0.0035 of a per-channel oracle, and outperforms the uniform SAITS pipeline (p=0.003). Its reconstruction performance is close to that of the strongest uniform pipelines, without a statistically significant improvement over them, and slightly below that of a single detector-imputer pair selected on validation data (0.978).
evidence_items.title: Experimental Artefacts for HARDIO: A Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator for Operational Data Quality in Instrumented Water Infrastructure

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps

evidence_items.summary: Parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is a cornerstone of their success, yet remains poorly understood. Existing knowledge benchmarks typically rely on predefined questions (e.g., "What is the birth date of M.L. King?"), evaluating only knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query, a problematic availability bias. In this paper, we introduce open knowledge evaluation, a new paradigm for benchmarking the stated knowledge of LLMs. Instead of asking narrow questions, it evaluates models on the knowledge they choose to surface in response to open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., "Tell me everything you know about M.L. King"). This shifts the focus from predefined answer retrieval toward characterizing the knowledge models naturally express. We instantiate this paradigm with BeQu (Beyond Questions), a benchmark of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification. Using BeQu, we evaluate a broad range of language models and analyze the effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. Data and leaderboard are available on this work's GitHub repository and at bequ.scads.ai, the benchmark website.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Questions: Evaluating the Stated Knowledge of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: CabbageRowSeg contains 929 RGB images at 1280 by 720 pixels and 1,281 cabbage mask occurrences from repeated views of approximately 60 physical plants in three rows during one field session. Row-organized data: R1 has 344 images and 542 masks; R2 has 295 images and 383 masks; R3 has 290 images and 356 masks. Each row has separate images and labels directories. Three row-disjoint folds are defined: F1 trains on R1, validates on R2 and tests on R3; F2 trains on R2, validates on R3 and tests on R1; F3 trains on R3, validates on R1 and tests on R2. The dataset-only package provides the original PNG images, YOLO polygon labels, existing COCO row annotations, fold definitions, image lists, documentation and integrity checksums. All original image and YOLO label bytes are unchanged from the previous release. The 929 frames and 1,281 annotations are repeated observations, not independent plants. Trained model checkpoints, pretrained weights, model configurations, prediction outputs, training logs and benchmark evaluation code are not included. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.
evidence_items.title: CabbageRowSeg: A Cross-Row Cabbage Instance Segmentation Dataset from Repeated Field Observations

evidence_items.summary: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $ρ\leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $ρ> 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.
evidence_items.title: IntReal: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Multimodal Interleaved Generation

evidence_items.summary: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.
evidence_items.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application

evidence_items.summary: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is a fundamental problem with applications in knowledge discovery, recommendation and beyond. Recent progress has highlighted the promise of combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Language Models (LMs) in order to leverage the complementary structural and semantic signals. However, due to the distinct inductive biases of GNNs and LMs, the design of an optimal fusion strategy remains an open research question. In this work, we present Bridge-LP, an intuitive, simple, efficient and theoretically grounded framework that unifies graph and language representations. It is built around three theoretically-justified design components: (D1) jumping connection of textual proximity, which enables robust LM training; (D2) compressed embedding, which encodes neighborhood information long exploited by classical link prediction heuristics, thereby enriching structural signals in a learnable way; and (D3) cache embedding training strategy, which reduces computational complexity. Together, these mechanisms establish an end-to-end cross-modal framework that scales to large graphs while capturing richer graph-text interactions. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, comparing against 40 existing models across 9 diverse datasets. Experiments show that Bridge-LP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering up to a 43.06% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and setting a new benchmark for language-graph integration.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Semantics and Structure: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Link Prediction on TAGs

evidence_items.summary: Bank-World is a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions. Completing banking work requires more than producing the right calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Bank-World tests these requirements through single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, we find that correct decisions often fail to become completed work. Agents charge fees twice, distribute the correct total in incorrect amounts among the recipients, and execute payments while approval is pending. Their strengths also differ: Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently. Bank-World makes these differences inspectable through task-level results and worked examples connecting source evidence, agent decisions, and simulated consequences. We retain the task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Bank-World: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Banking Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Reliable local search is essential for LLM agents to support everyday decisions and longer plans by finding places that meet users' needs at given times and locations. Yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgments in place attributes and reviews. We introduce ATLAS-Bench, a benchmark of 1,200 queries across three regions, expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews, and existing user profiles from the platform. Each query distinguishes mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgments, with supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. We also introduce ATLASBox, a standardized evaluation environment with search tools and a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Given a query, timestamp, and location, an agent searches place attributes and reviews to recommend evidence-supported options or report that no place meets all mandatory requirements. We evaluate answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%). These results highlight the challenge of satisfying individual requirements while providing usable recommendations across queries.
evidence_items.title: ATLAS-Bench: An Agentic Tool-Use Benchmark for Local Area Search

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it. Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.
evidence_items.title: AgentDecept: Benchmarking Deceptive Behavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents under Pressure

evidence_items.summary: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.
evidence_items.title: inkGround: Benchmarking Fine-grained Visual Grounding Capabilities of Vision-Language Models for Cursive Handwriting in the Wild

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
evidence_items.title: The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) Dataset : Auditing Socioeconomic and Demographic Disparities in LLM-Generated Financial Advice in India

evidence_items.summary: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.
evidence_items.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.
evidence_items.title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding

evidence_items.summary: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4

evidence_items.summary: LLM deception is often evaluated through fabricated claims, explicit lies, or strategic concealment. Yet misleading communication can also arise from selectively presenting true facts, for example, by omitting adverse evidence, softening unfavorable details, emphasizing favorable information, or replacing precise qualifications with vague language. Existing benchmarks largely overlook this subtler failure mode. We introduce JANUS, a benchmark for measuring goal-conditioned pragmatic distortion in fact-grounded LLM outputs. Each of its 160 scenarios, spanning 8 domains, provides a fixed pool of favorable and adverse facts and contrasts a neutral decision support with institutional conditioning, such as increasing adoption, or support despite potential harm to affected individuals or groups. By constraining outputs to the same fact pool, JANUS isolates misleading net impressions from hallucination and fabrication. Experiments across 12 LLMs reveal consistent goal-conditioned distortions, showing that current models remain sensitive to incentives and framing and lack robust safeguards against selectively misleading communication. We publicly release our corpus and code. https://github.com/PolydorosG/JANUS
evidence_items.title: JANUS: Evaluating Goal-Conditioned Distortion in Factually Grounded LLM Communication

evidence_items.summary: "Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used non-invasive sensing modality for continuous cardiovascular and physiological monitoring across clinical, laboratory, and wearable settings. While existing PPG datasets support a broad range of downstream tasks, they typically provide supervision in the form of numerical measurements or task-specific labels, limiting their compatibility with language-based interfaces and multimodal foundation models. In this work, we introduce PulseLM, a large-scale PPG-text question-answering dataset that bridges raw PPG waveforms and natural language through a unified closed-ended question-answering (QA) formulation. PulseLM aggregates PPG recordings from sixteen publicly available sources and harmonizes heterogeneous annotations into 12 downstream tasks. The dataset comprises over 1 million standardized 10-second PPG segments, associated with nearly 2.5 million question-answer pairs. We further define a reproducible data pipeline, training, and evaluation protocols and establish baseline benchmarks using multimodal PPG-aware large language models. PulseLM provides a standardized foundation for studying language-based physiological question answering, cross-dataset generalization, and scalable benchmarking of PPG-based multimodal models. We publicly release the dataset and code at https:\/\/huggingface.co\/datasets\/Manhph2211\/PulseLM and https:\/\/github.com\/manhph2211\/PULSE-LM, respectively."
evidence_items.title: "PulseLM: A Foundation Dataset and Benchmark for PPG-Text Learning"

evidence_items.summary: CryoAtlas v1.0 is a curated dataset and unified benchmark for research on automated protein atomic model building from cryo-EM density maps. Derived from EMDB and PDB records available up to March 2026, it contains 17,809 curated map–model–sequence entries, comprising 16,657 training entries and 1,152 test entries. Following map–model alignment, sequence mapping, and quality filtering, each entry provides paired experimental density maps, atomic structures, and protein sequences.This ScienceDB Package brings together three complementary components:Training set: 16,657 entries distributed across four non-overlapping parts. Each part preserves complete EMD entries and includes density maps, atomic structures in CIF format, protein sequences in FASTA format, and metadata identifying its contents.Test set: 1,152 entries organized into two subsets: the 618-target benchmark used for comparative evaluation in the paper and the remaining 534 test entries. The 618 targets are a subset of the complete test set, not an additional dataset.Benchmark resources: Predicted atomic structures, per-target evaluation results, split definitions, and supporting documentation for reproducing and analyzing the benchmark. Evaluation covers structural accuracy, model-to-map agreement, and stereochemical quality.The package provides a unified entry point for downloading the training and test data and accessing the accompanying benchmark resources. The dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International license (CC BY-NC 4.0); third-party materials retain their original licenses and attribution requirements. Additional documentation and code links are available at https://oulling.github.io/cryoatlas/.

evidence_items.summary: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial
evidence_items.title: A Unified Benchmark for Aerial-Enhanced Autonomous Driving: The KITScenes Aerial Dataset

evidence_items.summary: The early diagnosis of the vehicle malfunctions by the artificial intelligence (AI) is a promising way to reduce the breakdowns and the maintenance cost, but the reported accuracies in the literature are usually very high and they may not reflect the real use. In this paper, six machine learning classifiers were trained on the public Engine Fault DB dataset, which contains 55,999 records of 14 engine and exhaust variables under one normal and three fault conditions. The models were evaluated by two protocols, a random five-fold split and a blocked split in which the test segments represent unseen operating conditions. In addition, a random-effects meta-analysis of nine published studies was conducted. The results showed that the four-class accuracy was about 75% under the random split, and it dropped to between 41.17% and 66.92% under the blocked split. However, the detection of the fault against the normal state was almost perfect (AUC = 1.000), and when the two fault types which cannot be separated were merged, the accuracy became 98.22% with all the signals and 97.34% with six on-board signals only. The meta-analysis gave a pooled reported accuracy of 96.50% (95% CI 92.63% to 98.38%) with a very high heterogeneity (I2 = 98.47%). The findings indicate that, on this dataset, the AI models can detect the presence of a fault reliably, while the isolation of the fault type under new operating conditions remains difficult and it needs a stricter validation practice.
evidence_items.title: USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR THE EARLY DIAGNOSIS OF VEHICLE MALFUNCTIONS: A LEAKAGE-AWARE EVALUATION AND META-ANALYSIS

evidence_items.summary: Against the backdrop of policies promoting quality enhancement and excellence in vocational education alongside educational evaluation reforms, traditional classroom teaching assessments struggle to comprehensively reflect teaching quality due to limitations such as single-dimensional data and insufficient technological empowerment. To address this, this study constructs an AI-driven multimodal data fusion model for classroom teaching evaluation. This model encompasses a five-layer technical architecture—data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, metric calculation, and result feedback—integrating three types of multi-source heterogeneous information: teaching behavior data (based on DBSCAN clustering analysis), physiological state data (combined with ResNet-18 emotion recognition), and dynamic effect data (using TransE knowledge transfer evaluation). This enables comprehensive and precise diagnosis of the classroom teaching process. Empirical validation was conducted in smart classroom environments using S-T behavioral analysis, engagement curves, and the Rt-Ch model. Results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in identifying critical issues such as imbalanced teaching pacing and fluctuating student engagement, significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness and objectivity of evaluations. This research not only provides a replicable technical pathway for diagnosing vocational education classroom quality but also offers theoretical support and practical examples for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and educational assessment.
evidence_items.title: Construction and Empirical Research on Classroom Teaching Evaluation Model of Vocational Education Based on Artificial Intelligence Multimodal Data Fusion

evidence_items.summary: The global mobile application ecosystem has expanded rapidly, creating significant opportunities for the generation of revenue through user engagement and monetization strategies. Particularly, the segment of health & fitness apps has gained remarkable growth in user adoption and digital engagement. However, due to differences in purchasing power, digital adoption, and platform maturity, monetization efficiency varies widely across countries. This study examines the monetization gap and revenue potential with respect to the growth of active users in Health & Fitness mobile applications across five selected countries: India, China, Brazil, the United Kingdom, and the United States.With the help of panel data analysis, the study investigates the relationship between Monthly Active Users (MAU) and app revenue while also comparing the monetization gap between actual revenue and potential revenue, taking the United States as a benchmark for Average Revenue Per User (ARPU). The results suggest a statistically significant positive relationship between active user growth and revenue. However, an incredible monetization gap exists across emerging and developing markets, highlighting untapped revenue potential in countries other than the United States (US). This study enables us to assess the potential unrealised revenue across different markets.However, among the selected countries, a substantial monetization efficiency gap can be seen. Particularly, countries with relatively lower ARPU showed a considerable gap between actual and potential revenue. These findings highlight unexplored monetisation opportunities and recommend that Health & Fitness application providers explore market-specific strategies to improve revenue generation from existing user bases.
evidence_items.title: THE EVALUATING MONETIZATION GAPS AND REVENUE POTENTIAL IN HEALTH & FITNESS MOBILE APPS: A BENCHMARK PANEL ANALYSIS

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) — systems of autonomous, goal-directed software agents that plan, act, and coordinate with reduced human oversight — is moving from research prototypes toward applied data-science, perception, and decision-support pipelines. Yet the literature remains fragmented across largely disconnected strands: trust-aware orchestration of multimodal agents for visual classification, human adoption of autonomous AI agents, automated machine-learning (AutoML) pipelines for tabular data, and fully autonomous multi-agent systems for end-to-end data engineering. This review synthesizes four recent studies spanning these strands, together with the broader literature on multi-agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), large-language-model (LLM)-based knowledge-graph construction, and explainable AI, to build a unified picture of agentic AI as applied to intelligent data science. We propose a four-part taxonomy — perception-level trust orchestration, human adoption of agentic systems, automated feature/model pipelines, and autonomous data-engineering agents — and compare the reviewed studies on automation level, reasoning mechanism, knowledge representation, retrieval use, trust treatment, and evaluation methodology. The synthesis shows that individual components of an agentic data-science stack (confidence calibration, retrieval-grounded re-evaluation, automated feature synthesis, autonomous pipeline repair) have each demonstrated measurable gains in isolation, but no reviewed system couples them with a persistent, multimodal knowledge-graph layer, and adoption research indicates that user trust is not the dominant driver of usage intention — a finding with direct design implications.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Systems: A Review of Multi-Agent Reasoning, Trust, Orchestration, and Autonomous Data Science

evidence_items.summary: Background. Large healthcare organizations run many specialty applications, such as prescribing and dispensing, warehouse and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and billing, that depend on shared master data, chiefly the patient identifier (MRN) and the product identifier with its description. Standards such as HL7 v2 and FHIR can propagate a new or changed record from an origin system, but propagation failures (rejections, unmapped codes, missing mandatory fields, duplicates and timing dependencies) still rely on manual diagnosis and repair. The resulting gaps surface as held or failed transactions at the point of care and supply. Failures also arise without any interface error, when a record exists but its local build or configuration (for example location, charge or dispensing parameters) is incomplete. Objective. To specify a human-governed, closed-loop framework in which AI agents act as integration architect, builder, verifier and support engineer: designing field mappings, configuring receiving systems against an approved build standard, verifying cross-system data validity and local build completeness, and diagnosing and remediating propagation errors. Methods. The study followed a design-science approach. The synchronization gap is formalized, a seven-class failure taxonomy is derived, and a four-layer architecture (sense, reason, act, govern) is specified with tiered autonomy grounded in the Parasuraman-Sheridan-Wickens model of types and levels of automation. An explicit tier-decision rule and tool contracts are defined, verification checks are mapped to established electronic health record data quality frameworks, the closed loop is illustrated with a synthetic worked example, and a staged evaluation protocol with quantified safety gates is specified. Results.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Framework for Master Data Synchronization, Validation and Self-Healing Across Integrated Healthcare Information Systems

evidence_items.summary: security of retrieval-augmented language models is usually studied on one side at a time: the integrity of what enters the knowledge base, or the confidentiality of what leaves it. We show that the two sides are the ends of a single channel, and that treating them separately systematically overstates the protection obtained. A claim that survives ingestion is later retrieved and reproduced, so an adversary who can write documents controls part of the set from which the system is allowed to disclose; we call this poison-to-leak amplification. We formalise the channel, place claim units, attribution, admissibility and the leak surface on one footing, and specify an adversary that both writes and queries. We then prove an amplification bound showing that sentence anchoring turns the per-response disclosure ceiling into a policy invariant independent of the adversary share of the corpus; a composition cut showing that entailment-closed admissibility makes multi-turn composition gainless, together with a constructive lower bound for the case where closure fails; and a geometric bound on the cumulative success of a mutating attacker. From these we derive three design rules: verify at ingestion rather than enumerate at egress, deflect according to the value at stake, and refuse without explaining. The resulting framework, PROVE, gates admission on claim-unit provenance, restricts retrieval to a sensitivity-layered whitelist bound to review status, locks the evidence set and anchors every sentence to it, verifies the answer with a semi-supervised detector, and invalidates revoked entries within one update step. On SecKB-Bench, a constructive benchmark of 44,000 instances over seven attack families, PROVE reduces aggregate attack success from 90.1% to 1.82% and per-response leakage by 99.4%, while over-refusing less than any baseline, at 1.9 times the inference cost of the undefended pipeline.
evidence_items.title: SecKB-Bench and PROVE Reference Implementation: Benchmark Generator, Reference Code and Measurement Artifacts for Provenance-Gated Retrieval and Egress Containment in LLM Knowledge Systems

evidence_items.summary: Finding training data in million-scale machine learning repositories is a Web search problem where text relevance is not enough. A query couples a semantic training goal with constraints such as task, license, and training stage, and the metadata that would verify them are often missing. Text retrieval ranks dataset cards by similarity but cannot enforce hard constraints or follow the relations that reach a sparsely described dataset. Free-form tool-calling agents are more flexible, but the same model that picks a dataset also declares it a match, and nothing checks that the query's constraints are actually met. Neither approach establishes that the data it returns will improve model training. To address it, we propose AgenticDS, a contract-governed agentic framework in which every language model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it. The framework compiles a query into a typed search plan, executes it through admissible deterministic operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and verifies the provenance-grounded evidence before accepting a ranking or emitting a typed diagnosis that permits only local repairs. On HuDS-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, AgenticDS improves NDCG@10 by 25.7\% over the strongest dense--sparse hybrid and by 18.9\% over a commercial LLM agent. A controlled search-to-train study further shows that the datasets it retrieves give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code, and medicine. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/nju-websoft/AgenticDS.
evidence_items.title: From Intent to Improvement: Agentic Dataset Search for Better Model Training

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: To evaluate the accuracy of a large language model (LLM)-based agentic workflow to extract procedural data from free-text glaucoma clinical notes in the electronic health record (EHR). Design: Cross-sectional. Subjects: 1,250 subjects in the Bascom Palmer Ophthalmic Repository. Methods: Randomly sampled clinical notes from glaucoma encounters dated 2014 to 2024 were labeled by two glaucoma specialists (with an adjudicator as needed) for prior glaucoma-related procedures (name, date, details) and recommended future procedures (name, details). Notes were split into development (10%), validation (10%), and test (80%) sets. Five LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek-V4 Pro, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.1, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) were accessed in Microsoft Foundry through HIPAA-compliant containers. The extraction pipeline comprised a three-step agentic workflow (extraction, validation, and conditional revision) followed by text standardization. Detection of procedure data was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score. Among positive cases, performance was evaluated using exact-match accuracy and Jaccard Index (JI). Prior procedure labels were also compared with EHR glaucoma-related Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes. Main Outcome Measures: Accuracy, exact-match accuracy, JI. Results: A total of 1,984 (992 notes 2 eyes) labels were evaluated for each task in the test set. Prior and future procedures were identified in 1,057 (53.3%) and 152 (7.7%) eyes, respectively. Accuracy ranged from 0.965 (Grok) to 0.996 (Claude) for prior procedures and 0.969 (DeepSeek, Qwen)-0.978 (Claude) for future procedures. Among positive cases, exact-match accuracy ranged from 0.681 (Grok) to 0.890 (Claude) for prior procedures and 0.704 (Grok)-0.849 (Claude) for future procedures; JI ranged from 0.827 (Grok) to 0.956 (Claude) and 0.734 (Grok) to 0.883 (Claude), respectively.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Billing Codes: An Agentic Large Language Model Pipeline for Extracting Glaucoma Procedural Data from Free-Text Clinical Notes

evidence_items.summary: Vision–language models (VLMs) are often reported to outperform vision-only backbones for UAV power-line inspection. We examine that claim using ElecVQA-Bench, a 56,972-item resource derived from InsPLAD, and an audit of partition, evaluated items, label space, replication, input resolution, and side information. The original split has substantial source-photograph dependence and is used for paired diagnostic comparisons. Reported tower-disjoint retraining provides a limited check on new-tower performance within the same source dataset. On the original binary task, no difference is detected by a paired item-level test between the selected Swin and Qwen runs; this does not establish equivalence. Fine-grained results change with resolution, prompt information, class support, and seed. A 14-tower, three-seed comparison changes direction across seeds, and classes represented by only a few items substantially affect macro recall. The contribution is a reproducible task representation and reporting protocol for examining these dependencies, rather than a general ranking of model families or evidence of end-to-end UAV deployment.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy Evaluation of Vision–Language Models for UAV Power-Line Inspection: A Resolution- and Parity-Controlled Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Most language models are evaluated on only a few benchmarks: in our compilation of 401 models and 146 benchmark versions, the benchmark test coverage is only 8.3% on the most frequently used benchmarks. We present benchgap, a pipeline that estimates the missing scores without running any evaluations. It calibrates each benchmark against each same-capability benchmark on the models measured on both, fitting six monotone curve families and keeping the one with the lowest leave-one-out cross-validated error; multivariate mappings combine several sources. Calibrations never cross capability groups, must rise and never extrapolate beyond one fitted-range width; estimates never feed further estimates, and each carries its own cross-validated error and confidence level. In an end-to-end holdout of 15% of the measured scores, the pipeline fills 71% of the masked cells at 4.6 percentage points (pp) mean absolute error (MAE), 23% lower than a rank-2 matrix-completion baseline on the same cells; on the cells it leaves empty, the baseline's MAE is 11.8 pp. Realized MAE rises with the confidence level (3.1, 5.1 and 7.5 pp from high to low), but the realized root-mean-square error exceeds the claimed error labels, which are selected minima, by a factor of 1.4–1.7. We also quantify the harness tax, the disagreement between evaluation setups: on verified same-item-set pairs it is 8.7 pp on agentic benchmarks against 2.3 pp on tool-free ones, and enabling tools on Humanity's Last Exam raises the scores of all 11 models measured both ways, by 10.0 pp on average. Estimates are updated daily at https://benchgap.net.
evidence_items.title: Mind the Gap: Explicit Cross-Benchmark Calibrations for Estimating Missing LLM Evaluation Scores

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation

organizations: The University of British Columbia, Canada
evidence_items.summary: Automated program repair has traditionally focused on single-hunk defects, overlooking multi-hunk bugs that are prevalent in real-world systems. Repairing these bugs requires coordinated edits across multiple, disjoint code regions, posing substantially greater challenges. We present the first systematic study of LLM-driven coding agents ( Claude Code, Codex, Gemini-cli , and Qwen Code ) on this task. We evaluate these four state-of-the-art agents on 404 multi-hunk bugs from the PolyHunk dataset, yielding 1,616 repair trajectories for large-scale behavioral analysis. We employ fine-grained metrics to assess localization, repair accuracy, regression behavior, and operational dynamics across agents. We find that localization capability varies substantially, with Codex achieving the highest success rate (75.3%) and Qwen Code the lowest (40.4%). Repair accuracy also differs widely, ranging from 26.98% ( Qwen Code ) to 92.82% ( Claude Code ), and consistently declines with increasing bug dispersion and complexity (hunk divergence and spatial proximity). High-performing agents (Claude Code and Codex) demonstrate superior semantic consistency, achieving positive average regression reduction, whereas lower-performing agents often introduce new test failures. Notably, agents do not fail fast ; failed repairs consume substantially more resources (33%–440% more input tokens) and require longer execution time (35%–330%). Additionally, we developed Maple to provide agents with repository-level context. Empirical results show that Maple improves repair accuracy of Gemini-cli by ∼21% through enhanced localization. By analyzing fine-grained metrics and trajectory-level analysis, this study moves beyond accuracy to explain how coding agents localize, reason, and act during multi-hunk repair. Our findings underscore the impact of bug divergence and spatial proximity on multi-hunk repair success for coding agents.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Dynamics of Agentic Multi-Hunk Repair

evidence_items.summary: "Falls and unnoticed health emergencies are among the biggest threats to older adults living independently, yet few open datasets pair physiological vital signs with in-home safety events. This dataset merges two sources into 10,000 complete, one-to-one records. Each record links a device\u2019s heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, and oxygen saturation to its movement, fall, impact, location, and alert data. It is fully documented with a data dictionary, a governance audit, and a stratified 70\/15\/15 train\/validation\/test split that keeps the 3.49% alert rate in every partition.Our pre-modeling bias audit also found that every emergency alert (349 cases) occurs under the \u201cNo Movement\u201d state. We report this openly and give practical guidance on metrics, preprocessing, and sub-models to help prevent misleading results. We hope this lets researchers build and fairly benchmark fall-detection and caregiver-alert systems, and supports safer, more transparent AI for healthy ageing and independent living."

evidence_items.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.
evidence_items.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Prediction market platforms list thousands of contracts whose logical and economic connections are implicit in their resolution rules. We introduce a hierarchical agentic reduction (HAR) pipeline for constructing inspectable cross-event relation graphs and a behavioral benchmark for evaluating their alignment with market prices. This partitions a catalog of prediction markets, specified by question and resolution text, into topic clusters, applies typed LLM reasoning to small batches, and proposes signed relations with rationales between specific markets. We evaluate semantic relation graphs spanning eight monthly Kalshi catalogs (February to September 2026). Using data from 30.3 million trades, we compute a benchmark that compares linked pairs' signed price-change correlations with those of matched, unlinked controls from the same topic cluster on identical timestamps. Under full-sample and leave-first-week-out evaluation, relations identified by our pipeline exhibit higher signed Pearson price-change correlations, with statistical significance, than matched within-topic controls. This increase also appears under Spearman correlation and becomes larger among relations labeled as medium or high strength. This benchmark provides a criterion for comparing relation-discovery methods against observations beyond their input text, and our results indicate the ability of agentic AI and LLM reasoning to identify meaningful relations between individual markets in connected Web marketplaces.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI for Clustering and Relationship Discovery in Prediction Markets
