evidence_items.summary: The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) has been widely employed for feature selection in linear models and has also been extended to multi-layer perceptron (MLP) networks for both feature and group feature selection. Group-Lasso has also been used in feature selection using feed-forward neural networks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate the Group-Lasso principle into a Siamese network architecture for feature selection. Unlike existing approaches that primarily optimize classification accuracy, the proposed method aims to identify a compact subset of features that simultaneously preserves the intrinsic representation of the input data (the goal of Siamese network) and is expected to achieve high classification performance. Two variants of the proposed framework are developed: one based on the Euclidean distance and the other on a modified Jaccard similarity measure for real-valued vectors. The latter is specifically designed to improve feature selection for high?dimensional sparse data. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated on 12 benchmark datasets with feature dimensions ranging from 6 to 7070 using eight different classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Siamese Lasso framework consistently identifies compact and discriminative feature subsets maintaining competitive or superior classification performance, although the loss function used explicitly did not consider any regularizer to learn classification. In addition, the quality of the embeddings produced by these networks is assessed using manifold learning techniques such as UMAP and t-SNE.
evidence_items.title: Integrated Feature Selection for classification and Representation Learning with Group-Lasso Siamese Networks

evidence_items.summary: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.
evidence_items.title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click at a position on the screen; if the page has changed in the meantime, the click lands on an unintended element. Prior work treats the planning interval as the source of this risk. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, we find that the risk lies in page loading: 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. On these pages, waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial pages keep loading for longer: in the HTTP Archive's public crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of their HTML being parsed, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages, and 52% shifted their layout within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds, against 8% (61% against 26% among pages recorded in full). Where a check before the click is needed, as before irreversible actions and on pages that are still loading, a pixel comparison verifies the target's position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, and a 4B model matches the frontier model in verifying whether the previous action succeeded. We release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers: https://github.com/multimodal-ai-engineering/preflight-bench
evidence_items.title: What Does "Now" Mean to Your Computer-Use Agent? Stale Screenshots, Page Loads, and Which Check to Run Before a Click

evidence_items.summary: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.
evidence_items.title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Triple set prediction (TSP) is to recover missing relational triples in a knowledge graph by predicting the triple set instead of isolated links. Existing approaches predominantly rely on the subgraph-based completion paradigm, where the original graph is first partitioned into local subgraphs which are then independently completed. Such a paradigm suffers from fragmented structural reasoning, limited cross subgraph dependency modeling, and missing predictions across subgraphs. This paper proposes LatentDiff, a novel unified latent generative framework for TSP, which reformulates knowledge graph completion as latent space graph generation. LatentDiff first learns a compact latent representation using a relation-aware residual-quantized knowledge graph autoencoder, which encodes the whole graph into relation-aware latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks, and reconstructs triples through a factorized decoder. On top of this latent space, we introduce an observation-anchored latent graph diffusion model, where the target latent graph representation is perturbed toward the observed latent. The reverse process recovers missing triples through progressive latent denoising. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that LatentDiff outperforms the SOTA in terms of F_{tsp} by 5.4 percentage points on average. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LKGDiff-44A5.
evidence_items.title: From Local Recovery to Unified Generation: Discovering Triple Set in Knowledge Graphs via Observation-Anchored Latent Diffusion

evidence_items.summary: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.
evidence_items.title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are widely used in enterprises to access business systems and act on them in pursuit of a goal. However, fulfilling a user's request can cause harm. Era by Eon is a product that creates a digital twin of a company by simulating its business systems and data. Its simulators implement the programming interfaces of real products. Our benchmark uses ten of these systems, including Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira and Slack. We tested whether agents would carry out harmful business requests or trust misleading information in company records. We ran 19 models on 41 tasks three times, for 2,337 runs. Of the 2,304 runs that produced an answer, 918 (40%) contained a violation. The most common were false claims about actions or records (290 runs), following planted instructions (266) and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience (249). Every attempted change was recorded and blocked before it took effect. Misleading Slack messages caused 16 models to report an incorrect ticket status in 47 of 57 runs. No model was free of violations. The four best models violated in 22 to 24% of their runs. Yet one of them, Nova Pro, did the task correctly in only 30 runs.
evidence_items.title: An Alignment Benchmark for Enterprise Agents on Era by Eon

evidence_items.summary: The external sources retained in our non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed. The initial audit covered 39 sources through August 16, 2026, with later targeted updates through October 14. A purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint; a non-probability log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. We also execute a reduced pilot: 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence held fixed. Frozen automatic scoring identifies attacker-target adoption in $21/24$ raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition has no known adoptions and one unresolved response. The pilot measures output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions. Together, the framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, while leaving full retrieval and agent evaluation open.
evidence_items.title: Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Ball bounces and racket hits are the events from which tennis statistics are derived, and on monocular video the two are easy to confuse. We release a benchmark of 345 bounce and hit annotations at frame level on eight clips that mix broadcast, fixed elevated, phone and court-level viewpoints, with a frozen development and test split, a confusion-aware matcher, clip-level bootstrap intervals and a blind second annotation of three clips. On it we score supervised precise spotters with published broadcast weights, two zero-shot vision-language models, and RallyArb, an arbitration layer over a ball track and player poses that fits no parameter on event labels. The supervised spotters score near-perfectly on broadcast footage and almost nothing on phone and court-level footage, where the pooled bounce F1 of E2E-Spot is 0.130. RallyArb keeps a bounce F1 above 0.8 on the three phone and court-level clips, two of which were used to tune it, and finds 8 of 11 bounces on the held-out one, but it places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing. The vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint and miss the contact frame by about 0.1 s. Fine-tuned leave-one-clip-out from its broadcast weights, the spotter reaches about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips and stays at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle. The annotations, the evaluator and the frozen predictions of every scored row are released.
evidence_items.title: Can Event Detectors Leave the Broadcast Camera? Evidence from Tennis

evidence_items.summary: We present Protegrity-PII, a new PII detection model for structured and unstructured text. Protegrity-PII achieves a typed recall of 0.910 with a precision of 0.902 on a new benchmark we propose, PII-SCOPE. Our model processes text in 0.49 seconds per million characters at \$0.0005 per million characters on a single RTX 6000 using batched inference. Due in part to the expansive nature of the entity type taxonomy used in training, Protegrity-PII achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization when benchmarked against a selection of state of the art models and datasets.
evidence_items.title: Protegrity-PII Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Discharge summaries are crucial clinical documents containing the context of a patient's overall hospital stay, and are routinely reviewed by medical experts for patient readmission, ongoing care, and diagnostic decision-making. When reviewing them, medical experts often must iteratively synthesize information across multiple discharge summaries while verifying the evidence supporting each answer. Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical question answering, existing benchmarks do not sufficiently reflect this setting: they often evaluate exam-style medical knowledge or focus on single-turn question answering with limited evidence-grounding evaluation. We introduce EHRNote-ChatQA, the first benchmark for evidence-grounded multi-turn clinical question answering over patients' multiple discharge summaries. Built from de-identified MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, EHRNote-ChatQA contains 967 patient-level multi-turn samples spanning one to five notes and 16,072 medical-expert-verified QA pairs (8,036 content questions, each paired with an evidence-grounding question) across eight clinical categories. The benchmark is constructed through an expert-informed pipeline combining discharge-summary structuring schema, expert-curated multi-turn QA templates, and LLM-based generation, followed by review and revision of every single QA sample by 12 medical experts (11 physicians and 1 nurse). Benchmarking 24 proprietary and open-weight LLMs reveals several challenges, including that LLMs struggle more with evidence grounding than content answering, multi-turn errors compound across turns, and single-turn clinical QA performance does not reliably transfer to this setting. These findings establish EHRNote-ChatQA as a rigorous and practical benchmark for evaluating clinical QA systems.
evidence_items.title: EHRNote-ChatQA: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multi-Turn Clinical Question Answering over Longitudinal Discharge Summaries

evidence_items.summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promising performance in automated electrocardiogram interpretation, it remains unclear whether they perform actual step-by-step reasoning or just rely on superficial visual cues. To investigate this, we introduce ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark, a novel multi-turn evaluation framework comprising over 6,400 samples to systematically assess step- by-step reasoning across 17 core ECG diagnoses. Our comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models reveals a systematic shortfall in executing multi-step logical deduction. Although models possess the medical knowledge to retrieve clinical criteria for a diagnosis, they exhibit consistently low success rates in maintaining a complete reasoning chain, primarily failing to ground the corresponding ECG findings to the actual visual evidence in the ECG signal. These results demonstrate that current MLLMs bypass actual visual interpretation, highlighting a limitation in their visual grounding capabilities and motivating robust, reasoning-centric medical AI. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Jwoo5/ecg-reasoning-benchmark.
evidence_items.title: ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Capabilities in ECG Interpretation

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the research manuscript entitled “Numerical Verification and Empirical Evaluation of Tube Model Predictive Control for Adaptive Cruise Control under Bounded Longitudinal Disturbances.” The dataset supports the numerical verification and empirical evaluation of a Tube Model Predictive Control (Tube-MPC) approach for longitudinal Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) under bounded disturbances. It contains experimental summaries, per-step Tube-MPC records, paired performance comparisons against a Nominal Model Predictive Control (Nominal MPC) baseline, feasibility accounting, and stratified analyses across different scenarios, controller gains, and disturbance patterns. The experimental package includes 60 Tube-MPC experiment summaries and 60,000 per-step records, corresponding to 60 experiments with 1,000 requested simulation steps each. Paired performance analysis is restricted to 30 configurations completed by both controllers. The remaining 30 Nominal-MPC cases are retained in the feasibility accounting and are not represented as complete paired time-series comparisons. The experiments use a sampling period of 0.032 seconds and a bounded longitudinal acceleration disturbance set of [-2.238, 2.346] m/s². The dataset documents the numerical and experimental results under the specified plant model, disturbance assumptions, controller configurations, and simulation scenarios. The files are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and independent examination of the reported numerical results. The results should be interpreted within the stated experimental assumptions and should not be taken as evidence of universal controller superiority, physical vehicle validation, or a deterministic hard real-time guarantee.
evidence_items.title: Experimental Dataset for Numerical Verification and Empirical Evaluation of Tube Model Predictive Control for Adaptive Cruise Control under Bounded Longitudinal Disturbances

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides a curated collection of experimental multiaxial fatigue data compiled from scientific literature and reliable experimental sources. It has been developed within the framework of COST Action CA23109 – FABER (Fatigue Benchmark Repository), specifically as a contribution to Working Group 4.3 – Multiaxial High Cycle Fatigue, which addresses the influence of load multiaxiality on fatigue life estimation. The primary objective of this dataset is to provide a structured and traceable experimental reference for the benchmarking, assessment, and verification of existing and newly developed multiaxial fatigue life prediction criteria and methodologies. By bringing together experimental results from different sources within a consistent data structure, the repository aims to facilitate objective comparisons between prediction approaches and support the critical assessment of their accuracy, applicability, and limitations under different multiaxial loading conditions. The collection covers different material systems, specimen geometries, and combinations of loading components, including axial (tension–compression or bending), torsional, and internal pressure loading. Both the loading conditions and the corresponding stress states are documented, including mean and alternating stress components, load ratios, loading frequencies, and phase relationships. Where the available information allows, the database also provides the specimen geometry and the corresponding applied forces, moments, and internal pressures, enabling the reconstruction of experimental loading conditions and supporting finite element-based investigations. The database is organized into material-specific Excel workbooks, each including a summary of the relevant material properties and experimental sources, together with a detailed record of individual fatigue tests.
evidence_items.title: Multiaxial Fatigue Dataset for Benchmark and Verification of Multiaxial Criteria (COST Action CA23109 - WG4.3 - Fatigue Estimation. Load Multiaxiality Effect)

evidence_items.summary: The 2026 FIFA World Cup expanded the international tournament format from 32 to 48 national teams, increasing the schedule from 64 to 104 matches across 16 host venues in Canada, Mexico, and the United States (concluding on July 19, 2026, with Spain defeating Argentina 1–0 in the Final). While demand for quantitative sports analytics continues to grow, open-access football datasets frequently lack relational constraints, complete squad lineups, standardized player identifiers, or expected goals (xG) metrics. Here, we present the FIFA World Cup 2026 Master Dataset, a 3rd Normal Form (3NF) relational database capturing all 104 matches, 48 qualified national teams, 16 host venues, 28 match officials, 1,248 registered squad players, 5,408 match lineup records (26 registered players per team per fixture), 601 chronological match events, tactical team statistics, expected goals (xG), and pre-engineered predictive feature matrices. Data was collected continuously during the 39-day tournament via an automated multi-source ingestion pipeline, normalized into 12 relational tables, and verified using an automated 10-stage programmatic test suite alongside an empirical spot-check of 30 matches against official FIFA Technical Study Group (TSG) reports (2,397 / 2,400 concordant telemetry points; 99.88% empirical accuracy). Distributed across CSV, Snappy-compressed Apache Parquet, and SQLite formats (sqlite fifa world cup 2026.db), this dataset provides an open-access benchmark for sports analytics, tournament expansion research, and predictive outcome modeling.
evidence_items.title: The FIFA World Cup 2026 Master Dataset: A Normalized 3NF Relational Benchmark of the Expanded 48-Team International Football Tournament

evidence_items.summary: Background/Aims: To date, some large language models (LLMs), such as Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4-omni (ChatGPT-4o), can process images through visual transformer patching. An LLM analysis was conducted to assess the ability of ChatGPT-4o to assign the Mayo endoscopic score (MES). Methods: A selection set of high-quality endoscopic frames was identified to compare 4 input models to select the most performant, confirmed in an extended set of 304 frames. Concordance with the evaluation by expert endoscopists was assessed. Results: Only one of the pre-tested models demonstrated significant concordance (κ = 0.232, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.167 to 0.296, <i>P</i>= 0.003; ρ = 0.36, <i>P</i>= 0.011), with a mean bias of –0.26 ± 1.192 (95% CI, –2.596 to 2.076). This was confirmed in the extended set (κ = 0.260, 95% CI = 0.195 to 0.324, <i>P</i>< 0.001; ρ = 0.288, <i>P</i>< 0.001). The absolute concordance for the selected model was 44% and 45.3% in the selection and extended sets, respectively. For the identification of moderately-to-severely active disease, a sensitivity of 73% (95% CI, 60% to 82%), specificity of 60% (95% CI, 54% to 66%), positive predictive value of 32% (95% CI, 25% to 40%), and negative predictive value of 90% (95% CI, 84% to 93%) were identified. Conclusions: ChatGPT-4o shows a mild potential in evaluating MES in endoscopic frames, but further refinements are mandatory.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of the Mayo endoscopic score in ulcerative colitis using a multimodal large language model: a human-blinded accuracy study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Existing environmental and health information systems typically provide isolated data streams, requiring users to interpret heterogeneous information sources without personalized guidance. Residents and health providers of urban regions with complex environmental conditions, such as the Salt Lake Valley, frequently seek timely, location-specific information about weather, air quality, and their associated health impacts, but may find it difficult to integrate this information in their decision-making, precluding the effective translation of valuable environmental health information into action. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline that delivers evidence-grounded, neighborhood-scale responses to health-related environmental questions raised lay persons by dynamically orchestrating authoritative weather, neighborhood-scale environmental observations, air quality, and health-evidence resources. Methods: We developed an agentic AI pipeline using LangGraph and OpenAI large language models to interpret natural language queries, select and invoke relevant external tools, retrieve real-time environmental data and evidence-based health guidance, and synthesize responses. The pipeline integrates multiple authoritative resources, including weather forecasts, air-quality observations, geospatial services, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module built from asthma-related clinical guidance. The system incorporates fallback mechanisms to improve robustness when external services are unavailable. We evaluated the pipeline using a curated benchmark of representative user questions, assessing tool-needed recognition, correct tool selection, avoidance of irrelevant tools, parameter mapping, analytic pathway selection, and incorporation of tool outputs into the final response.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Pipeline for an Evidence-Grounded Environmental Health Public Information System: Development and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Recent AI systems can autonomously execute scientific workflows and empirical software tasks. We investigate whether an autonomous agent can use evaluation feedback to iteratively develop a scientific model. To address this question, we developed AutoResearch-MLIP, a research protocol in which the agent follows predefined instructions to propose, implement, and evaluate MLIP designs, with outcomes carried forward to guide subsequent iterations. Starting from a simple pair-distance MLIP, each generation selects a parent model by balancing exploration and exploitation, while structured design records guide subsequent proposals. Across 40 generations, the agent explores MLIP designs spanning local message passing, radial representations, scalar-vector states, body-order terms, residual readouts, long-range-inspired terms, and periodic image-offset graph construction. The final G40 model is competitive with established MLIP baselines in post hoc benchmarks. These results show that, within predefined rules, an autonomous agent can use evaluation feedback to iteratively improve MLIP implementations.

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
evidence_items.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly formalized as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which an agent maximizes expected reward while keeping its expected cumulative cost below a specified safety bound. Existing safe RL benchmarks predominantly report whether an algorithm is safe on average, following this expectation-based guarantee. We argue that this convention is insufficient to reliably characterize an algorithm's true safety: it fails to capture how often and how severely the safety bound is violated, whether this holds consistently across tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior is representative of behavior of the final converged policy. Therefore, we introduce (i) evaluation metrics for safe RL that address each of these concerns and in addition allow for aggregation across tasks and safety bounds. We furthermore define (ii) a safety tier system to systematically categorize and compare algorithms in terms of safety and reliability at both training and for a final policy. Using this framework, we provide (iii) an empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks. Our results show that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal information the other metrics cannot. We therefore recommend reporting all three jointly, rather than compressing this information into a single value, as is common practice. We provide SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support the reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Metrics for Safe Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Intrusion detection models deployed on resource-constrained networks face two practical difficulties that are often studied in isolation. Attack behaviour changes over time, so a model trained once tends to lose accuracy as the traffic distribution shifts, and the volume of generated alerts can exceed the capacity of the analysts who must act on them. This study presents a detection framework that addresses both concerns within a single streaming pipeline. An incremental ensemble classifier is paired with an adaptive windowing drift monitor that governs when the model updates, and a predictive-uncertainty gate decides whether each flagged flow is raised as an automated alert or routed to analyst review. The framework was evaluated on the CICIDS2017 flow dataset using a chronological prequential protocol that preserves the order of traffic and exposes the model to shifting attack mixes. Under this protocol the proposed framework reached a prequential F1-score of 0.951 for the attack class, compared with 0.936 for an adaptive random forest and 0.862 for a static offline model. After each induced distribution change the static model settled at a lower accuracy, whereas the proposed framework returned to its prior range within a few evaluation windows. At a gating threshold of 0.40 the precision of automated alerts rose to 0.976 while 15 percent of flows were referred for review. The detector operated within a 256 MB memory profile and sustained roughly 1,390 flows per second. These results describe behaviour for the evaluated dataset and configuration and are not presented as evidence of universal improvement.
evidence_items.title: A DRIFT-AWARE CYBERATTACK DETECTION FRAMEWORK FOR RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED NETWORKS USING ADAPTIVE LEARNING AND UNCERTAINTY-BASED ALERTS

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the item-level evaluation of 30 Spanish-language mobile health (mHealth) applications aimed at promoting healthy lifestyles in three domains: nutrition (n = 5), mindfulness (n = 15) and habit tracking (n = 10). Apps were identified in the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store in February 2024 using the keywords “nutrition”, “mindfulness” and “habit tracker” (n = 560), screened against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria (35 apps included), and re-assessed in a replication search in October 2026 (5 apps excluded). Each app was scored with the validated iSYScore instrument (popular interest, 0–11; trust and quality, 0–18; usefulness, 0–18; overall score 0–47; acceptable quality ≥ 23.5 points) and with an artificial intelligence (AI) mapping framework based on World Health Organization ethical guidance and the European Union AI Act (0–18 points; risk class: non-AI system or limited-risk AI). Thirteen apps (43.3%) reached acceptable quality, and 12 (40.0%) were classified as limited-risk AI systems. Scores were assigned independently by expert reviewers in nutrition, psychology and digital health, with discrepancies resolved by consensus.

evidence_items.summary: Degree-aware evaluation can expose sampling bias in synthetic-lethality prediction, but how should a model's degree-controlled benchmark score inform its use in experimental screening? We link fixed-prediction benchmark interventions to retrieval in measured experimental pools. Across five gene-disjoint folds, replacing Random test negatives with degree-matched negatives changed mean AUROC from 0.782 to 0.501 for SLMGAE, 0.721 to 0.502 for GCATSL, 0.656 to 0.492 for GRSMF, and 0.376 to 0.519 for SL2MF. The opposite movement of SL2MF shows that test composition can suppress as well as inflate discrimination. Crossed training-testing experiments and a three-seed diagnostic separated these changes from degeneration during matched GCATSL training. In four measured screens, the same Random-trained SLMGAE states retrieved 21 SPIDR hits in 198 selections, versus 8.00 expected under random ranking: a 2.62-fold enrichment despite near-chance matched-test AUROC (within-task Holm-adjusted p=0.0008). Comparable robust primary gains were not established in HAP1, a 27-cell-line compendium, or SCHEMATIC, where limited coverage and dependent observations constrain inference. A separate in-domain HAP1 control retrieved 11 hits versus 2.02 expected. These results establish an empirical dissociation between degree-controlled benchmark discrimination and experimental hit retrieval. A near-chance matched-test score can coexist with useful experimental prioritization. Our released evaluation suite makes both properties measurable from saved predictions, alongside checks of training viability and task coverage.
evidence_items.title: Separating benchmark discrimination from experimental retrieval in synthetic-lethality prediction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rest on classical comparators that lack the same features, on simulation alone, and on unreported hardware cost. QBioBench is a benchmark of quantum machine learning on peripheral biosignals that holds quantum and classical models to the same features and reports calibration and hardware cost. It comprises three clinical tasks, 12-lead ECG diagnosis (PTB-XL), single-lead apnea detection (Apnea-ECG), and wearable stress detection, each reduced to six to eight shared dimensions. A factorial grid of projected and fidelity quantum kernels and variational classifiers is screened in noisy simulation, and the promoted configurations are evaluated in an exploratory study on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor on the full test pools of 510 apnea minutes and 512 PTB-XL records. Every prediction is recovered from the device records, intervals resample recordings or patients, and classical baselines are trained on the same units and tested on the same executed inputs. No quantum model reaches its matched support vector machine in ROC-AUC on either primary task, and none is separably better in balanced accuracy. The angle-encoded fidelity and projected kernels reach ROC-AUC 0.697 and 0.693 on apnea, paired differences of − 0.127 and − 0.119 to the support vector machine, and both are classical by construction, since the entangling layer of the encoding cancels from the fidelity kernel and leaves closed-form local expectations in the projected kernel. A variational classifier comes closest, reaching 0.797 on apnea (difference − 0.012 , 95% interval [ − 0.052 , + 0.027 ] ), and falls to chance without its two-qubit gates. Test sets of the size that circuit budgets favor are unreliable, as random 80-minute subsets of the apnea pool give the fidelity kernel a central 95% range of ROC-AUC from 0.589 to 0.797. Readout mitigation changed ROC-AUC by at most 0.015.
evidence_items.title: QBioBench: benchmark of quantum machine learning for peripheral biosignals on real hardware

evidence_items.summary: Overview This repository provides the computational code, numerical input configurations, and verification datasets supporting the research entitled "Automated Staged Finite Element Modeling and Eccentric Prestress Coupling Verification for Railway Continuous Box Girders." The study develops a physics-consistent automated staged beam–truss finite element framework for railway prestressed concrete continuous box girders. The framework distinguishes numerical solvability, model credibility, and candidate acceptability, with particular emphasis on eccentric prestress transfer, construction-stage state management, and structural and geometric constraint diagnostics. Computational Case The reference case is a three-span (32 + 48 + 32) m railway prestressed concrete continuous box girder. The numerical model is implemented using Python and OpenSeesPy and contains 5,289 nodes, 5,144 finite elements, and 116 registered longitudinal tendon paths. Verification Scope The supporting materials cover the following computational assessments: Analytical P–Pe verification of eccentric tendon–girder force and moment transfer. Full-model tendon–girder connection registration and topology audits. Bridge-scale comparisons between equalDOF legacy and rigidLink-beam coupling formulations. Prestress-input sensitivity analyses of the rigidLink-beam formulation using scaling factors of 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2. An independently assembled two-dimensional Euler–Bernoulli benchmark for the representative ZK external-load increment. Construction-stage response auditing and geometric constructability screening. Geometric checking-point refinement and archived candidate-feedback diagnostics. Reproducibility and Limitations The reference numerical analyses adopt small-deformation, linear-elastic modeling assumptions.
evidence_items.title: Source Code and Verification Dataset for Automated Staged FE Modeling and Eccentric Prestress Coupling in Railway Continuous Box Girders

evidence_items.summary: This analysis examines how execution settings relate to performance variability in scientific computing benchmarks, addressing the reliability of computational comparisons across servers. It uses 120,564 CloudLab executions recorded between 2018 and 2019, aggregated into 6,588 server and configuration groups across 183 servers. Matched comparisons estimate differences in execution time coefficients of variation within the same server and benchmark, with confidence intervals calculated across server averages. Enabled frequency scaling is associated with 0.130 percentage points higher variability, while the 20-thread setting is associated with 0.137 percentage points higher variability than one thread. Both confidence intervals exclude zero under the stated inference assumptions. Benchmark comparisons reveal different patterns, including a negative average thread difference for CG, indicating that the overall association is not uniform across workloads. Sensitivity checks retaining groups with at least 10 executions and excluding the server with the highest mean variability preserve the positive average differences. The findings support workload specific performance evaluation and encourage computing operators to report dispersion alongside mean execution time. The associations do not establish causal mechanisms or numerical reproducibility.
evidence_items.title: HARDWARE CONFIGURATION AND EXECUTION TIME VARIABILITY IN SCIENTIFIC COMPUTING RESEARCH BENCHMARKS ACROSS CLOUDLAB SERVERS

It uses published results from a curated benchmark released in 2020, comprising 27 observations across nine tools and three vulnerability categories. Descriptive comparisons measure matched detections relative to annotated vulnerabilities within each category. Mean detection across tools was 8.2% for access control, 21.7% for arithmetic, and 47.2% for reentrancy. Mythril achieved the highest arithmetic coverage at 68.2%, while Slither led reentrancy detection at 87.5% and shared the highest access control coverage at 21.1%. No tool led across all categories, indicating that aggregate rankings can conceal differences relevant to audit planning. These results describe benchmark coverage without identifying causal mechanisms or establishing performance beyond the selected annotations. The contribution is a focused secondary comparison that makes category specific detection differences explicit. For international auditing practice, the evidence supports evaluating coverage against relevant vulnerability classes and reporting the scope of automated checks alongside their results.
evidence_items.title: COMPARING AUTOMATED DETECTION OF ACCESS CONTROL, ARITHMETIC, AND REENTRANCY VULNERABILITIES IN CURATED ETHEREUM SMART CONTRACTS

evidence_items.summary: Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training, nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles, every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p < 10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed numbers.

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise data pipelines have grown in scale and interdependency faster than the operational practices used to maintain them. Pipeline failures are still predominantly diagnosed and remediated by human engineers reading logs, tracing lineage, and applying tacit knowledge, which produces long mean-time-to-recovery and concentrates institutional knowledge in a small number of individuals. This paper proposes an agentic architecture in which large language model (LLM) agents, constrained by explicit tool interfaces and policy guardrails, perform continuous monitoring, root-cause triage, and bounded remediation of production data pipelines. The framework specifies five cooperating agent roles — Observer, Diagnostician, Remediator, Verifier, and Orchestrator — operating over a shared state store containing pipeline metadata, lineage graphs, data-quality expectations, and incident history. We define a capability-tiering model that maps each remediation action to one of four autonomy levels (observe, recommend, act-with-approval, act-autonomously), and we describe a human-in-the-loop governance layer providing approval routing, immutable action logging, and rollback. We further propose an evaluation protocol covering task success rate, mean-time-to-detection, mean-time-to-recovery, false-remediation rate, and escalation precision, together with a reference workload derived from common ingestion, transformation, and schema-evolution failure modes. The paper concludes by analysing failure modes specific to agentic operation — hallucinated root causes, unsafe tool invocation, reward-free drift, and accountability gaps — and argues that autonomy must be earned incrementally through measured reliability rather than granted by architectural default.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Driven Data Engineering: A Framework for Self-Directed Enterprise Data Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances the factual accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs), standard implementations face critical enterprise vulnerabilities including vector embedding side-channel leakage, unauthorized privilege escalation, prompt injection susceptibility, unmonitored autonomous execution, and lack of regulatory observability. This paper introduces Enterprise Agentic RAG, an innovative production-grade architecture combining a stateful 7-agent orchestration workflow (LangGraph) with strict Pre-Search Vector Payload Filtering across four security clearance tiers (Restricted, Confidential, Internal, and Public). The proposed system integrates hybrid retrieval combining BM25 lexical scoring with dense vector cosine similarity (Qdrant HNSW indexing) optimized through Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Furthermore, the pipeline features an autonomous Tool Agent capable of policy-validated, AES-256 encrypted corporate email dispatch, an egress Data Loss Prevention (DLP) firewall preventing unauthorized data exfiltration, deterministic multi-layered guardrails neutralizing adversarial prompt injections, jailbreaks, PII exposures, and sensitive credential leaks, alongside real-time Prometheus operational telemetry and an immutable audit logging engine. Empirical benchmarking demonstrates 100% RBAC pre-filter precision, zero vector embedding leakage across privilege boundaries, 98.7% average groundedness score, sub-150ms end-to-end orchestration latency, and 100% interception of adversarial injection and DLP egress violations, establishing an enterprise-ready framework for secure corporate intelligence synthesis.
evidence_items.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG with Pre-Search Role-Based Access Control, Multi-Layered Guardrails, and Operational Telemetry

evidence_items.summary: Background Parkinson’s disease (PD) requires both disease-specific knowledge and contextual clinical reasoning. However, most evaluations of medical large language models (LLMs) emphasize closed-ended questions and factual accuracy, providing limited insight into broader dimensions of performance on professional PD tasks. Methods Nine contemporary LLMs were evaluated using a 200-item English-language professional PD benchmark spanning five clinical domains, four difficulty levels, and multiple question formats. Responses were assessed for expert-rated factual accuracy, clinical reasoning, Global Quality Scale (GQS), and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Results The nine models generated 1,800 responses. Between-model separation was minimal for expert-rated factual accuracy (Kendall’ s W = 0.031) but greater for FKGL (W = 0.235), Clinical Reasoning (W = 0.256), and GQS (W = 0.301). Between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy was small for closed-ended questions (W = 0.020, p = 0.001) but greater for open-ended questions (W = 0.121, p &lt; 0.001). Expert-rated factual accuracy remained weakly discriminative across PD domains and difficulty levels, while GQS showed the greatest domain-specific separation in Safety &amp; Ethics (W = 0.431). Flagship variants consistently showed higher Clinical Reasoning and GQS, but not uniformly higher factual accuracy. Conclusion Contemporary LLMs showed limited between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy within this benchmark and scoring framework, whereas greater differentiation emerged in open-ended tasks, clinical reasoning, overall response quality, and readability. Multidimensional evaluation may therefore provide a more informative characterization of model performance and help inform task-specific model selection and oversight in medical applications.
evidence_items.title: Comparative performance of nine large language models on professional Parkinson’s disease tasks: a multidimensional benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting‐edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data‐driven overview of the “Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education” (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general‐purpose LLMs. While high‐income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a “democratizing effect” on upper‐middle‐income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open‐source models. Global equity critically demands cross‐border collaboration and inclusive datasets.
evidence_items.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education

organizations: Yuvakshetra Institute of Management Studies, Palakkad, India
evidence_items.summary: Learners on a massive open online course (MOOC) platform choose from thousands of courses, and recommender systems have long been used to narrow that choice. Since 2022 a new ingredient has arrived: large language models, which can read course descriptions, rank candidates from a prompt, hold a conversation about a learner's goals and write a reason for each suggestion. This review asks what those models change for course recommendation and how much of the claimed benefit has been shown on educational data. We sketch the earlier MOOC recommenders and their datasets only briefly, then take four roles of a language model in turn: text encoder, ranker, conversational recommender and explanation writer. Most of the evidence for these roles comes from films, books and retail products. Studies on course data exist, but they are few, recent and almost all offline. We then look at how such systems are evaluated, where offline scores mislead, and the risks that weigh most in education: invented courses or prerequisites, popularity and provider bias, unequal treatment of learner groups, privacy and cost. This is a review of published work. No new experiment is reported.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Course Recommendation on Mooc Platforms: A Review

evidence_items.summary: Framing research has long relied on human annotation, but many aspects of framing – especially framing functions such as defining problems, identifying causes, making moral evaluations, or proposing solutions are difficult to label consistently and at scale. We demonstrate that large language models can reliably identify these framing functions, achieving levels of agreement comparable to those of human annotators. We evaluate three state-of-the-art models (GPT-5, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek) alongside three trained human coders on a new dataset of social media posts about electric-vehicles, a highly topical and contested issue that holds many interpretations. This setting provides a strong test of both agreement and meaningful disagreement in framing-function annotation. Across models and humans, we find not only substantial convergence but also patterns of valid disagreement – differences that reflect legitimate alternative interpretations rather than annotation error. Recognising and preserving these cases enhances construct validity and provides a more realistic portrayal of how framing functions operate in contested debates. Our results demonstrate that large language models can scale framing function analysis while capturing the variability inherent in human interpretation, enabling forms of communication research that were previously impractical with human-only coding.
evidence_items.title: Agreement Helps, Disagreement Matters: Scaling Framing Function Annotation With Large Language Models

organizations: Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering in Skopje
evidence_items.summary: Experimental ADMET profiling is essential to drug discovery but incredibly costly that only a fraction of candidate molecules can be measured, motivating active learning to prioritize informative compounds. However, evidence remains limited on how acquisition strategies and uncertainty estimators interact across different ADMET tasks. Thus, we present a protocol-matched benchmark of seven acquisition strategies and two uncertainty approaches (Deep Ensembles and MC Dropout) across eight ADMET regression endpoints. Our framework combines molecular prediction, uncertainty estimation, batch aquisition and empirically calibrated prediction intervals, with a strict chemotype split to evaluate generalization to held-out chemical groups. The results reveal that active-learning benefits were endpoint and strategy-dependent, with the broadest favorable pattern observed for solubility and diversity-aware approaches showing the most consistently favorable behavior across endpoints. Deep Ensembles achieved lower mean RMSE than MC Dropout in 45 of 56 matched comparisons, although this predictive advantage did not consistently translate into better acquisition. Post-hoc analyses associated this disconnect with weak uncertainty-error alignment and reduced chemotype coverage in selected batches. This benchmark offers a reproducible basis for choosing endpoint-specific acquisition strategies, assessing prediction quality alongside computational cost, and designing prospective studies with matched random controls.
evidence_items.title: When Does Active Learning Improve ADMET Prediction? A Multi-Endpoint Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Background: The acyclic monoterpene β-myrcene (CAS No. 123-35-3) is a food flavoring classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as “possibly carcinogenic to humans” (Group 2B) based on neoplastic findings in rodents. Its toxicological relevance is closely tied to its metabolic fate: CYP-mediated epoxidation yields reactive intermediates that are rapidly detoxified to diols, and the weight of evidence provides no indication of DNA reactivity. Separately, a threshold-based dose–response approach was adopted as a pragmatic default assumption, consistent with EFSA and JECFA practice, rather than as an inferred mode of action. This study therefore combined this metabolic understanding with benchmark dose–response (BMD) modeling to derive a health-based guidance value (HBGV). Methods: Tumor-incidence data from the two-year National Toxicology Program (NTP) gavage studies in rats and mice were modeled with BMDS Online version 25.1 from US EPA, following international guidelines. Doses administered on five days per week were converted to time-weighted average daily doses before modeling. The 1000 mg/kg dose group was excluded from modeling because survival at that dose indicated that the maximum tolerated dose had been exceeded. A benchmark response (BMR) of 10% extra risk and a 95% lower confidence limit were applied. Models were evaluated by goodness of fit and Akaike information criterion (AIC). Results: The BMDL10 of 18.2 mg/kg b.w./day for hepatocellular adenoma (including multiple) in male mice was selected as the point of departure (POD). Applying an uncertainty factor of 100 yielded an acceptable daily intake (ADI) of 0.18 mg/kg b.w./day, equivalent to 180 µg/kg b.w./day. At estimated flavoring intakes of 3–138 µg/kg b.w./day, the ratio of the ADI to the estimated intake, which is not a margin of exposure in the EFSA sense, ranged from approximately 60 to 1.3.
evidence_items.title: Metabolic Fate, Mode-of-Action Considerations, and Benchmark-Dose Risk Assessment of the Natural Monoterpene β-Myrcene

evidence_items.summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo EM) relies on mature computational tools, but experts must still inspect intermediate results, choose among alternative processing routes, and decide when earlier choices should be revised. Here we present CryoPilot, a system of two language model agents that carries cryo-EM data from raw micrographs through three-dimensional reconstruction to validated atomic models. Rather than executing a predefined pipeline, its reconstruction agent evaluates intermediate images and quantitative diagnostics, selects and parameterizes CryoSPARC jobs, tests alternative strategies, compares their outcomes, and retains, revises, or reverts decisions accordingly. A persistent programming environment and session database preserve the complete processing history, making each decision traceable and allowing multi day workflows to proceed with minimal human intervention. Its modeling agent determines map handedness, builds atomic models with CryoZeta, removes regions the density does not support, and optimizes each model by testing refinement steps against map fit, geometry, and DAQ, a measure of local model to map agreement. Across nine public EMPIAR datasets, eight reconstructions reached 2.61 to 3.51 A resolution, and refined models from seven maps agreed with reference structures to within 0.4 to 4.9 A Calpha; RMSD. For a challenging alpha latrocrustotoxin dataset, a single change of particle picking strategy that we suggested enabled CryoPilot to improve the reconstruction from 5.9 to 4.15 A. CryoPilot establishes an adaptive and auditable framework for agent-driven cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence_items.title: Agentic cryo-EM structure determination with CryoPilot

organizations: Institut Supérieur d'Informatique et des Technologies de Communication de Hammam Sousse
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Learning-based intrusion detection produces verdicts operators must simply trust: the audit record is mutable and no independent party endorses the decision. We present BAg-IDS, a distributed detection architecture in which autonomous agents detect, independently re-check, and co-sign every remediation-triggering verdict on a Hyperledger Fabric ledger before it is acted upon, placing certification on the decision path rather than in an after-the-fact log. A calibrated, reliability-weighted ensemble with a reject option feeds the quorum; language-model and governed human-in-the-loop tiers handle escalation. The full stack is implemented and every number measured. Selective certification raises accuracy from 96.6% to 99.7% (0.04% false-positive rate) at 87.3% coverage on CICIDS2017, and reaches 99.98% on the independent GeNIS 2025 corpus while deferring 0.14% of flows. A 360-alert benchmark shows the ~ 2 s consensus latency is structural: one write per key per block forces K votes across at least K blocks, a bound no submission strategy removes.
evidence_items.title: BAg-IDS: A Blockchain-Enabled Agentic AI Architecture for Trustworthy Intrusion Detection

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and business analytics are increasingly converging to support automated financial decision making, yet integrated frameworks combining business intelligence with taxation remain limited. This study develops an autonomous cloud-based decision-support framework integrating agentic AI, business analytics, Income Tax intelligence, and GST intelligence. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data processing, business analytics, banking analysis, tax screening, GST rule evaluation, anomaly detection, orchestration, and decision support. Empirical evaluation used integrated commercial and banking records to assess sales, profitability, payment behavior, cash flow, and transaction-risk indicators. Results showed total sales of ₹437,771, recorded profit of ₹36,963, bank credits of ₹420,570.51, and bank debits of ₹422,089.90. UPI represented 45.07% of integrated records, while anomaly screening identified 152 high-value sales observations and 135 high-value banking transactions. Income Tax and GST outputs were generated as rule-based intelligence indicators rather than statutory assessments because direct return variables were unavailable. The proposed architecture demonstrates the feasibility of combining autonomous agents, cloud-enabled analytics, financial monitoring, and tax-oriented screening while retaining explainability, auditability, and human oversight for consequential decisions. The framework provides a scalable foundation for future enterprise deployment, real-time integration, and compliance-oriented financial intelligence applications.
evidence_items.title: An Autonomous Cloud-Based Decision Support Framework Integrating Agentic AI, Business Analytics, Income Tax, and GST Intelligence
