evidence_items.summary: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
evidence_items.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions

evidence_items.summary: As preferences, goals, and facts change, LLM agents must use the current state while earlier versions remain in context. Yet they can answer with an old value of the same variable, a failure that we call stale binding. To study when models use outdated information and why, we introduce Controlled In-Context Memory (CICM), a benchmark for tracking and using updated information in conversations and agent logs. We observe that even frontier reasoning models can fail to recover the current state. We find that in open-source models probes can still recover the updated value when the model answers with an old one, pointing to a failure to select information that remains available. Component tests in Qwen and Pythia identify a mechanism for this selection failure: attention drift, where attention favors old values over the current one when producing an answer. We study a one-layer transformer to mathematically understand how this phenomenon happens: when attention scores are similar, several old values can together receive more attention than the current value. Guided by this explanation, we redirect attention toward the current value without further training. When the current value is requested directly, adjusting this intervention for each input corrects most old-value errors across various model families while preserving nearly all initially correct answers. Reliable context management therefore requires more than remembering updated information: models must use it to guide their answers.
evidence_items.title: When Context Changes: Understanding Update Failures in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Instruction-guided video editing requires executing a requested change while preserving the source video's appearance and temporal structure. We present SemantiScene-Edit, a video editor that couples a multimodal encoder with a pretrained video diffusion transformer. The encoder jointly processes source frames and the editing instruction, and learnable queries convey their semantic context to the generator through a trainable connector and cross-attention. A complementary visual pathway concatenates source-video latents with noisy target latents before patch embedding, supplying dense spatial and temporal information for content preservation. We train the model with flow matching and a three-stage image--video curriculum comprising semantic alignment, joint adaptation, and high-resolution refinement. To support training, we construct over 1.2 million instruction-conditioned video-editing records covering object addition, removal, replacement, and attribute modification. We also construct a 100-case benchmark for evaluating instruction execution, source preservation, temporal consistency, and visual quality. Comparative experiments show that SemantiScene-Edit effectively follows editing instructions while retaining source content. At inference, the model requires only a source video and a natural-language instruction.
evidence_items.title: SemantiScene-Edit: Expert-Synthesized Supervision and Dual-Path Source Conditioning for Instruction-Based Video Editing

evidence_items.summary: When we speak of recursive self-improvement (RSI), are we speaking of a phenomenon, a mechanism, or a prospect? Towards autonomous and evolving intelligence, RSI is being claimed at many scales, while no single framework that formally describes these emerging instances exists. Its counterpart in the classical realm, iterative policy improvement, is characterized by generalized policy iteration (GPI), a framework of broad applicability with well-understood theoretical properties, but only where the update principle and the evaluation base lie outside the agent. In this paper, we propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that describes iterative policy improvement and RSI as two cases of a single learning paradigm. GAI defines the agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a system and models the learning process as a cycle of agent evaluation and agent improvement. Two pivotal dials then distinguish the instances, in particular the systems that self-identify as RSI in recent work: whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent and whether the standard it is measured against is grounded outside it. The former dial delineates the boundary between GPI and RSI, and the latter determines a system's polarity as anchored, goal drift, or fully self-referential. Moreover, we use these coordinates to place existing systems on the same two axes and make the defects of recursive self-improvement statable one condition at a time. We see this paper as a first step toward exploring a formal characterization of RSI that rests on the classical account, makes existing systems comparable, and provides a principled basis for analyzing and designing new ones.
evidence_items.title: Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in peer review at major AI conferences, yet novelty remains a persistent weak point. Existing benchmarks assess novelty as a single holistic score, making it difficult to diagnose which dimension a model misjudges or whether its evidence is faithful. We present NovGauge, a human-anchored benchmark for fine-grained novelty assessment diagnosis. The benchmark contains 619 paper pairs and 50 multi-paper sets, drawn from two expert sources: ICLR reviewer overlap claims and survey co-citations. Instances are independently labeled along three dimensions: task, problem, and method, capturing application goals, technical challenges, and solution approaches. We propose a cascading diagnostic pipeline that verifies per-dimension correctness, evidence grounding, and logical support. Evaluation of 18 LLMs shows hallucination rates ranging from 0% to 39% across dimensions, and among non-hallucinated correct-positive judgments, over 70% cite evidence fails to logically support the stated reason. The best-performing model, GPT-5.5, achieves 43-72% Verified F1 across dimensions, while most models retain less than half of their raw F1 after faithfulness verification. These results suggest that current LLMs remain far from reliable scientific novelty assessment, particularly when correctness is conditioned on faithful evidence grounding.
evidence_items.title: NovGauge: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Diagnosing LLMs' Capability in Paper Novelty Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Discovery---formulating novel generalizations---is a central part of the scientific process. Despite its importance, there is a gap in the current AI benchmark landscape, with few benchmarks directly probing the capacity for discovering new knowledge with experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. To address this gap, we release a new benchmark: DiG-bench (Discovery in Games). DiG-bench consists of a set of 70 independent games. Each game is encoded as a short string and has unique transformation rules that must be discovered through interaction and experimentation. The levels of the game present a series of challenges to test whether the rules have been discovered, where the win conditions for each level are also unknown. We provide games at seven tiers of difficulty for AI agents. The lowest tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, while the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt. A subset of 21 games is released publicly, and the remainder is held private for secure evaluation.
evidence_items.title: DiG-bench: Discovery in Games

evidence_items.summary: Memory-agent evaluations report fixed-snapshot accuracy or retrieval quality, but these scores do not show whether evidence remains usable as irrelevant sessions (sessions not annotated as task-relevant evidence for the query) accumulate. We present a scale-conditioned evaluation protocol for agent memory under evidence-preserving growth: for each query, task evidence is held fixed while irrelevant sessions are added. The protocol logs agent-memory trajectories and reports four diagnostics: budget-compliant reliability, tail memory-call burden, failure-regime decomposition, and the usable-scale boundary where reliability falls below the target. Applied to LongMemEval and LoCoMo across flat, planar, and hierarchical memory interfaces, the protocol shows reliability loss is not a single phenomenon. On LongMemEval, HippoRAG stays within the two-call budget but loses 16-20 percentage points in budget-compliant reliability as irrelevant sessions are added; LiCoMemory's observed failures depend strongly on the agent, with Qwen3-8B exceeding the budget while Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B remain reliable in the tested range. The result supports a framework for making scalable-memory claims conditional on agent, interface, scale range, and interaction budget. Code and evaluation artifacts: https://github.com/AndyLu666/memory-at-scale
evidence_items.title: When Stored Evidence Stops Being Usable: Scale-Conditioned Evaluation of Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Strict anonymity of model responses is a key for the reliability of voting-based leaderboards, such as LM Arena. While prior studies have attempted to compromise this assumption using simple statistical features like TF-IDF or bag-ofwords, these methods often lack the discriminative power to distinguish between stylistically similar or within-family models. To overcome these limitations and expose the severity of vulnerability, we introduce INTERPOL, a model-driven identification framework that learns to distinguish target models from others using interpolated preference data. Specifically, INTERPOL captures deep stylistic patterns that superficial statistical features miss by synthesizing hard negative samples through model interpolation and employing an adaptive curriculum learning strategy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that INTERPOL significantly outperforms existing baselines in identification accuracy. Furthermore, we quantify the real-world threat of our findings through ranking manipulation simulations on Arena battle data.
evidence_items.title: InterPol: De-anonymizing LM Arena via Interpolated Preference Learning

evidence_items.summary: Crafting effective reward signals remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) for complex reasoning. Existing methods for automated reward optimization search with a fixed proposer which never learns from its costly trials. We present Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (DERL), a dual-training framework for autonomous discovery of reward structures. An outer-loop proposer composes a reward from task primitives, and an inner policy trains with this reward. The proposer itself learns by policy gradient from the validation performance of the inner policy. Thus, DERL utilizes past-trial feedback to shape its reward-proposal distribution, an empirical meta-gradient of task success. We validate DERL on embodied (ALFWorld), scientific (ScienceWorld), and mathematical (GSM8K, MATH) reasoning. On multi-turn agent benchmarks, DERL outperforms strong baselines, significantly on out-of-distribution tasks. In mathematics, DERL improves on the outcome reward where directly added primitives hurt. Further analyses under matched compute show that our proposer effectively captures the meta-gradient to discover useful reward signals.
evidence_items.title: Dual-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Automated Reward Design

evidence_items.summary: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
evidence_items.title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills

evidence_items.summary: Many everyday robot manipulation skills are affordance-dependent, with success determined by whether the robot contacts the functional object region required by the subsequent action. Current simulation data generators obtain contacts from generic grasp estimators or per-object manual contact annotations, but generic estimators rank stable grasps without task semantics and often select contacts that are misaligned with the downstream action, while manual contact annotations must be rewritten for each new object and task. To solve these challenges, we introduce AffordSim, a scalable data generator and benchmark that integrates open-vocabulary 3D affordance prediction into simulation-based trajectory generation. Given a natural-language task description, AffordSim synthesizes a task-relevant scene, emits affordance queries, grounds them on object surfaces, samples region-conditioned grasps, and selects executable candidates with motion planning. It further randomizes object pose, texture, lighting, image noise, and cross-viewpoint backgrounds for sim-to-real transfer. We instantiate AffordSim as a 50-task benchmark across diverse manipulation skills, five robot embodiments, and 500+ rigid and articulated objects. AffordSim achieves 93% of the trajectory collection success rate of manual contact annotations on affordance-critical tasks and 89% on hard composite tasks. Vision-language-action policies trained on AffordSim data transfer zero-shot to a real Franka FR3, reaching 24% average success.
evidence_items.title: AffordSim: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark for Affordance-Aware Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Experiment 4: Best A3 Transfer to Dataset 3 1. Overview This Zenodo repository provides research materials associated with Experiment 4: Transfer of the Best A3 Multi-Source Annotation-Refinement Strategy to Dataset 3 , conducted as part of the study: Distribution-Aware Dataset Design and Multi-Source Pseudo-Label Refinement for Tree Species Detection in Dense Forest Aerial Imagery The experiment investigates the transferability of the selected Best A3 (A3-native, native) annotation-refinement pathway to a distribution-aware, image-disjoint Dataset 3 constructed using a 60/20/20 training, validation, and test partitioning strategy based on Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). The central objective is to determine whether multi-source pseudo-label refinement improves four-class tree-species detection in dense forest aerial RGB imagery and whether incorporating additional pseudo-labeled images into the final detector-training set provides further benefits. The experimental framework employs Faster R-CNN with a ResNet-50 Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) as the downstream detection architecture. 2. Dataset Description The dataset is derived from high-resolution SWISSIMAGE aerial RGB imagery of Swiss forests, with an approximate ground sampling distance of 10 cm. The labeled image collection contains 4,438 aerial image patches and 10,128 expert-provided bounding-box annotations covering four tree species: C1: Norway spruce ( Picea abies )- C2: Silver fir ( Abies alba )- C3: Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris )- C4: European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) Dataset 3 follows a 60/20/20 image-disjoint partitioning scheme: | Subset | Number of Images ||---|---:|| Training | 2,663 || Validation | 888 || Test | 887 || Total | 4,438 | The experiment uses expert-provided annotations as the reference labels. Accepted model-generated pseudo-labels are incorporated into the training data, while the validation and test annotations remain unchanged.

evidence_items.summary: Plastic contamination of aquatic systems is a critical environmental issue, yet the evidence base remains fragmented across marine and freshwater environments due to incompatible measurement protocols. This study synthesizes secondary data to characterize the sources, transport pathways, spatial distribution, and temporal trends of micro- and macroplastic contamination, evaluating the comparability of published observations. The design is quantitative and comparative, relying entirely on existing datasets without primary sampling. Four secondary datasets were analyzed: UNEP and Chassignet et al. (2021) on marine plastic sources and transport; the Atlas of Ocean Microplastics (AOMI) on ocean surface microplastic density; the OECD Global Plastics Outlook database on plastic use, waste, leakage, and projections; and the NOAA NCEI Marine Microplastics Database on microplastic concentrations across marine matrices. Variables regarding concentration, waste generation, leakage, location, particle density, transport pathways, and reporting periods were extracted, standardized, and structured while retaining sampling and analytical metadata. The synthesis confirms that rivers act simultaneously as plastic accumulation zones and primary conduits to oceans, microplastics permeate all aquatic compartments, and freshwater systems remain undersampled relative to oceans. Methodological heterogeneity including variations in sampling gear, mesh aperture, size definitions, laboratory preparation, counting conventions, and model-derived data prevents direct interchangeability of reported values. Harmonized sampling protocols and reporting conventions are necessary for data aggregation and operational monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Micro and Macroplastic Contamination Analysis and Detection in Water Bodies: A Secondary Data Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: GeoAI-THM Studio is a free, noncommercial agent that turns a plain-language request (English or Korean) into an OpenGeoSys 6.5.8 model of subsurface heat conduction, groundwater flow, heat transport, solute transport, consolidation, thermal stress or coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical processes, runs it, and reports values computed from the run, checking each number in the answer against the run, the model inputs and the request. The language model edits a typed model tree through tools ordered by a state machine; a translator writes the OpenGeoSys input; a configuration is computed only after its verification cases have passed with the installed versions; and an output guardrail rejects answers whose numbers cannot be traced to the run, the model inputs or the request. This record contains: (1) the source code of the geoai-thm-studio Python package 0.1.1 (command-line chat, Model Context Protocol server, tools, translator, mesh step, verification cases, examples, instructions and knowledge base) with its tests; (2) the verification record of 27 cases against exact solutions, official OpenGeoSys benchmarks and, for a demonstration configuration, consistency checks (21 within 1 %, all within 2.5 %); (3) the scenarios, scripts and result files of the tests with small language models (a Claude Haiku stand-in and a final check with gpt-6-luna and gpt-6.1-terra), the recomputation audit and the point-source element-size sweep; (4) the technical note in English and Korean (PDF); (5) the preprint submitted to the ESS Open Archive (in moderation) (PDF, the v0.1.0 text); (6) the installable wheel geoai thm studio-0.1.1. Install: pip install "geoai-thm-studio[mesh-gmsh] @ git+https://github.com/geoaialignment/geoai-thm-studio@v0.1.1" (macOS 15 or later on Apple Silicon, Linux x86 64 tested only under emulation; Python 3.12). Repeat the verification with thmstudio verify; the scripts in scripts/ rebuild every reported number from results/ and runs/.

evidence_items.summary: ZJU BESS Time-Series, Semantic Reports, and Downstream Benchmark Suite Overview This dataset suite provides large-scale, real-world operational time series from a lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS), together with structured, human-readable operational reports and three ready-to-use downstream benchmarks. Unlike battery datasets designed for a single prediction target, this release connects three levels of battery intelligence: 1. Raw multivariate operation data from 28 battery modules; 2. Structured semantic reports describing module- and cell-level temporal behavior; 3. Task-specific labels for SOC prediction, operational-anomaly analysis, and charge/discharge decision support. The suite is intended to support research at the intersection of battery management, multivariate time-series analysis, explainable AI, and large language models (LLMs). It enables both conventional numerical modeling and emerging time-series-to-language research without requiring users to reconstruct benchmark samples from the full operational archive. The operational records cover a six-month period from December 1, 2023 to May 31, 2024 . Measurements are sampled at one-minute intervals. All public identifiers are anonymized and independently assigned within the released datasets.
evidence_items.title: ZJU-o and Downstream Benchmark Datasets: Battery Operational Time Series and Semantic Reports for LLM-Assisted O&M

evidence_items.summary: MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench is a derived dataset of 320 curated hospitalization cases (v1.0.0) built from MIMIC-IV (v3.1) and MIMIC-IV-Note (v2.2). Each case is a structured patient profile drawn from the discharge documentation of a single hospitalization, covering diagnoses, medications, follow-up instructions, and post-discharge care plans. Cases were sampled from adult patients evenly across 16 diagnostic chapters, which combine matching ICD-9 and ICD-10 chapters into a single version-neutral grouping. Profiles were extracted from the structured tables and discharge notes with a large language model and manually reviewed against the source notes. Each case is paired with simulated-patient traits (personality, education level, health literacy, and medical-history recall). The dataset was developed for DischargeBench, a framework that simulates conversations in which an LLM educator explains discharge instructions to a simulated patient. The release also includes the complete simulation records of eight closed- and open-source models (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-4B, MedGemma-27b-text-it, and MedGemma-4b-it), each run five times on every case. The simulation code and prompts are publicly available on the DischargeBench GitHub repository.

evidence_items.summary: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a Platonic Representation Theorem: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--good views--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with bad views, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.
evidence_items.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs

evidence_items.summary: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
evidence_items.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps

evidence_items.summary: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.
evidence_items.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating human-AI co-design requires testing whether coding agents can translate real users' multimodal requests into working application revisions. We introduce Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of 273 tasks curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions. Its two tracks, Multimodal Editing (ME) and Repository Editing (RE), cover localized edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs and coordinated repository revisions. Tasks span three capability dimensions: Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation. The tasks pair normalized requests and runnable pre-edit applications with 2,331 hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria. Our judge-then-refute protocol grades criteria using source and browser evidence, challenges positive verdicts with a separate LLM verifier, and audits visual and interaction claims without gold code or target screenshots. Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. Co-Design Bench provides a testbed for studying the gap between partial requirement satisfaction and complete task success under agentic execution for real-user application revisions.
evidence_items.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models

evidence_items.summary: Blockchain forensics is adversarial and open-ended: money launderers split, swap, and bridge funds, cut their trail at mixers or custodial services, and change tactics from one incident to the next. Investigators must keep adapting their tracing in response. Yet the immutability of public ledgers preserves every recorded movement in public view, making much of the investigation independently verifiable. We introduce ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that makes evidence-backed fund tracing a verifiable agent task, in which every claimed movement must cite ledger records the agent retrieved. A case-to-task pipeline builds well-posed tasks across ledgers: conservative rules halt tracing wherever the records leave a continuation unresolved, and each task's reference graph is the answer those rules determine. Built from real laundering activity, the tasks combine multi-hop transfers, DeFi exchanges, cross-chain round trips, custodial and mixer deposits, and address poisoning. We also propose the ABF agent harness, built around a working memory, and evaluate it alongside general-purpose agents and fixed-order tracers. The harness reaches 75% edge recall, against 47% for Codex with the same model and 10% for Claude Code, which loses recall to overconfidence: it cites records it left unretrieved. Compared with fixed-order tracers, the harness acquires evidence faster than the best of them early in the budget and recognizes undisclosed custodial services that they walk past (89% vs. 0%), with 98% fidelity. However, agents tend to stop early and lose recall on larger tasks, which holds their final recall below the best tracer. Beyond exposing these gaps, ABF-Bench opens blockchain forensics to LLM agents as a verifiable domain, where the verdicts that score agents also offer potential training signals.
evidence_items.title: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics

evidence_items.summary: Dados de apoio ao estudo bibliométrico sobre a interseção entre Inteligência Artificial (IA), jornalismo e dimensão ambiental. Os registos foram identificados na Scopus (n=139) e na Web of Science - Core Collection (n=73), interrogando título, resumo e palavras-chave na interseção de três blocos temáticos, IA, jornalismo e ambiente, para o período 2000–2026. Após harmonização dos metadados e desduplicação (por DOI e, na ausência deste, por título normalizado), foram removidos 69 duplicados, resultando um corpus de 143 registos únicos (70 exclusivos da Scopus, 16 exclusivos da Web of Science e 57 comuns). Cada registo foi triado por título, resumo e palavras-chave e classificado quanto ao grau em que considera o impacto ambiental do uso de IA. O pacote inclui: a lista limpa dos 143 registos do corpus (xlsx e csv); as exportações em bruto das duas bases; o corpus consolidado e classificado, com as folhas Summary, Merged Unique, Removed Duplicates e Env Screening (classificação temática A/B/C e descritor ambiental que recuperou cada registo); e os codebooks dos instrumentos de análise. O conjunto permite replicar a constituição do corpus, a desduplicação, a caracterização bibliométrica e a classificação temática que sustenta o resultado central do estudo. Os ficheiros em bruto são as exportações originais das bases, disponibilizados para transparência; os direitos sobre os metadados pertencem às respetivas bases e editoras.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models often deviate from the target word count when following length constraints such as “generate X words.” Existing studies mostly focus on content quality, while paying relatively less attention to format control, especially the accuracy of length control. To address this issue, this study builds a Chinese text generation benchmark covering 5 topics and 4 word-count levels, and evaluates three representative models: DeepSeek-V3, Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen2.5), and Kimi. Based on this, a lightweight post-processing framework, LAPP (Length-Aware Post-Processing), is proposed. When the output is too long, LAPP uses sentence-level intelligent truncation; when the output is too short, it calls Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct for semantics-preserving expansion, and controls the length error within ±10% through iterative correction. The experimental results show that the original average deviation rates of the three models are 11.93%–38.70%, which are reduced to about 5% after LAPP correction, and the pass rate increases from 20%–70% to 85%–100%. The semantic preservation results show an average BERTScore of 0.97 between the corrected and original texts, suggesting that the framework improves length control while largely keeping the original meaning. This study shows that the “rough generation + precise correction” approach is effective for word-count control, and offers a low-cost, transferable way to improve the instruction-following ability of large language models.
evidence_items.title: Research on the Length Controllability of Chinese Large Language Model Outputs Based on Post-Processing Correction

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how prompt design influences the quality of large language model (LLM)-generated business-to-business (B2B) market research outputs. It also proposes a switch-point governance mechanism for converting LLM-generated drafts into decision-ready market intelligence artefacts. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an exploratory pilot evaluation of three market-facing LLM-based tools: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity AI. The tools are compared across three benchmark B2B market research tasks and three prompt types: basic, context-augmented and role-specific. In total, 81 outputs were generated. A role-specific benchmark subset of 27 outputs was then assessed using automated metrics and blinded human ratings. The automated metrics included relevance through cosine similarity, reference overlap through ROUGE-F1, cross-run semantic stability, latency, token length and readability through Flesch Reading Ease. Human evaluators rated the outputs on relevance, completeness, factuality, instruction-following and insightfulness. One-way ANOVA and non-parametric checks are reported as exploratory task-level tests, not as confirmatory evidence of model superiority. Findings Role-specific prompts produced the strongest descriptive scores in this pilot setting. Within the benchmark subset, Gemini showed the strongest observed profile, with higher average relevance, reference overlap and semantic stability, along with lower latency. ChatGPT produced relevant outputs but tended to generate longer and less readable drafts. Perplexity generated concise and readable summaries, but its outputs were less aligned with the reference brief and decision-facing requirements. Human ratings followed a similar descriptive pattern. Cross-run semantic stability showed directional alignment with higher decision-readiness ratings, offering preliminary support for P1.
evidence_items.title: Advancing value creation in B2B market research – a human–AI collaboration framework for large language model

organizations: Jan Evangelista Purkyně University in Ústí nad Labem
evidence_items.summary: Abstract User reviews of mobile applications provide a source of citizen feedback on digital public services, yet their automated analysis in non-English settings is constrained by the limited availability of domain-adapted classifiers. This study develops and evaluates a documented procedure for three-class sentiment classification of Czech reviews of government mobile applications using a large language model without task-specific fine-tuning. The corpus comprised 10,198 reviews of six applications. An adjudicated human reference was created for a stratified random sample of 500 reviews, and LLM performance was compared with a majority-class baseline, two lexicon-based methods, and two readily deployable encoder-based transfer models. The validation included five repeated runs under identical settings and an analysis of classification errors. Across five GPT-5.6 Sol validation runs, mean accuracy was 93.0%, mean macro-F1 was 0.827, and mean Cohen's kappa was 0.857. Macro-F1 ranged from 0.814 to 0.845, while agreement among the five runs was high (Fleiss' kappa = 0.918). The neutral class was the most challenging, with most disagreements occurring at its boundaries with negative and positive sentiment. In the full corpus, 65.9% of reviews were classified as negative, 7.9% as neutral, and 26.2% as positive. Textual sentiment was strongly associated with star ratings but was not identical to them. These findings provide corpus-specific evidence that a standardized LLM procedure can help analyze short-form non-english citizen feedback. They also underscore the need for human reference labels, stability checks, and precise documentation of the model, prompt, settings, and execution workflow.
evidence_items.title: Sentiment Analysis of Government Mobile App Reviews: Validating Zero-Shot Classification with a Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Examination of retinal images provides a non-invasive means to assess the body's microvascular system, with vessel morphology linked to ocular and systemic diseases. QUARTZ (QUantitative Analysis of Retinal vessel Topology and siZe) is an automated, artificial intelligence-enabled retinal vasculometry system designed for processing large-scale retinal image datasets, including over 4 million images from within the National Health Service, to facilitate epidemiological studies. The system is uniquely capable of extracting useful information from lower quality images, including those which are partially illuminated, enabling analysis of a greater proportion of images. To enhance cross-dataset generalisation of the system from an earlier dataset-tailored approach, this work leverages 26 annotated retinal image datasets spanning diverse demographics, diseases, camera types, and imaging protocols. Evaluation on the external EPIC-Norfolk dataset demonstrates robust performance with F1 scores of 0.8305, 0.8477, 0.8741, 0.9532, and 0.8677 for arteriole, venule, vessel, optic disc, and optic cup segmentation, respectively, and 0.9197 for image quality classification. The cross-dataset generalisation approach demonstrated increased performance for arteriole/venule segmentation and optic disc segmentation. However, improvements in performance were not observed for optic cup segmentation, or for image quality classification. An online tool is provided to support wider adoption and reproducible biomarker research across diverse populations and imaging settings. In addition, the new public CHASE-AV database is introduced for arteriole and venule segmentation.
evidence_items.title: QUARTZ: Cross-Dataset Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Retinal Vasculometry

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) may be increasingly positioned to strengthen autism spectrum disorder (ASD) assessment by improving scalability, consistency, and workflow efficiency across settings that serve children. Traditional diagnostic tools such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2) and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) require extensive clinician preparation and are difficult to implement in many contexts, which contributes to delays and uneven access. This article provides a detailed review of how AI methods can be embedded within existing evaluation procedures. Computer vision, speech analysis, natural language processing, predictive modeling, and multimodal fusion techniques are examined as tools that can support observation, interviewing, scoring, and documentation. A central contribution is a conceptual framework organized around structured signal extraction, interpretable and modular models, and strong safeguards that guide responsible use. Key challenges include bias, variation in data quality, and appropriate alignment with clinical judgment. The article offers a foundation for clinicians and researchers seeking to integrate AI within ASD assessment workflows.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Autism Assessment: A Conceptual Framework for Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Integration

evidence_items.summary: The study of the ecological interactions within microbial communities is crucial for gaining deeper insights into community ensemble and evolution, enabling targeted modification of the community’s functionality. Many inference approaches have been developed to derive ecological associations. Here, we focus on co-occurrence computational methods, in which associations are inferred from metagenomic abundance data by measuring the statistical dependence between species counts across different sampled populations. The limitations in culture-based experiments have hindered the ability to assess these methods’ validity, leading to scarce application in metagenomics studies. To provide a comprehensive assessment of network inference method performance, we benchmark 18 different computational approaches across a broad spectrum of experimental scenarios. We use synthetic 16S rDNA-seq count data generated from known underlying interaction networks, enabling systematic and controlled evaluation. The benchmark spans scenarios varying in numbers of species and samples, sample richness, sequencing depth, and interaction network structure. We evaluated the performance of the methods both in terms of accuracy of the inferred network, using various metrics from binary classification theory and metrics coming from network science, and in terms of computational burden. We found that methods have valid results only in a restricted, and often unrealistic, field of application, whereas their effectiveness diminishes with more realistic simulation parameters. Our findings highlight the limits of the co-occurrence-based approach and the need for further development in microbial ecological association inference.
evidence_items.title: From 16S rDNA-seq count data to microbial interactions: A comprehensive benchmark of co-occurrence network inference methods

evidence_items.summary: Context. Detached eclipsing binaries (DEBs) provide model-independent measurements of stellar masses and radii, which are essential for testing stellar-evolution models and calibrating space-based photometric missions. Aims. We aim to deliver ultra-precise fundamental parameters for the DEB UX Men and to assess its suitability as a benchmark for upcoming missions such as PLATO . We evaluate the temporal stability of the photometric solutions and the way intrinsic stellar variability and instrumental systematics affect the derived parameters. Methods. We analysed 31 TESS sectors (∼882 d) with the LIGHTKURVE package, and detrended spot-induced variability. Light-curve modelling was performed independently with JKTEBOP and ALLESFITTER . Radial velocities from HARPS (HAM/EGGS), FEROS, CORALIE, and UCLES were extracted via TODCOR and fitted with a Keplerian orbit. Spectral disentangling (5350–5800 Å) yielded individual component spectra, which were processed with ISPEC to determine T eff , [M/H], and micro- and macroturbulence. Eclipse-timing variations were examined through O-C diagrams. We also used multi-band photometry to determine the fluxes, flux ratios, and ultimately, to measure the photometric T eff . Results. We obtained masses of M A = 1.2300 ± 0.0012 M ⊙ , M B = 1.1946 ± 0.0012 M ⊙ and radii of R A = 1.3605 ± 0.0031 R ⊙ , R B = 1.2801 ± 0.0069 R ⊙ , with a sub-percent precision. Uncertainties were found to be dominated by systematic effects coming from (weak) stellar activity. The metallicity estimates are [ M / H ] A = 0.02 ± 0.13 dex and [ M / H ] B = 0.07 ± 0.10 dex. An isochrone fitting yielded a consistent age of τ = 2.75 ± 0.13 Gyr. The system exhibits a ∼673-day periodicity in eclipse-timing variations, likely due to stellar activity, with no evidence of a third body. Conclusions.
evidence_items.title: UX Men: Detached eclipsing binary as a benchmark candidate

evidence_items.summary: Vibration measurements from civil structures inherently contain fundamental dynamic characteristics and are widely used to monitor structural behavior to inform condition assessment. Machine learning, particularly unsupervised deep learning models, has demonstrated strong potential in automatically learning patterns from baseline vibration data and detecting anomalous structural behaviors. Complex multiscale temporal patterns may arise in structural responses, particularly under rapidly varying external loads, potentially leading to obscured anomalies and reduced anomaly detection accuracy. The primary contribution of the study is the establishment of a benchmark dataset from vibration tests of a laboratory-scale truss bridge. The benchmark vibration dataset contains structural responses under stationary and moving-load excitations, including multilocation and multilevel structural anomaly scenarios. The established dataset can be further used as a benchmark for moving load identification, modal identification, structural model updating, and structural anomaly detection, among others. Additionally, a multiscale pattern learning approach for vibration-based structural anomaly detection by integrating the TimeMixer network with the one-class support vector machine (TimeMixer-OCSVM) is introduced. The methodological contribution lies in establishing a TimeMixer-OCSVM validation baseline, which demonstrates the capability of the benchmark dataset to support anomaly detection studies. The TimeMixer model is adopted to learn multiscale patterns from structural vibration data, improving the anomaly detection performance under varying external excitations. The constructed benchmark dataset is used to validate the proposed method, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying structural anomalies. Compared to the other typical methods, the proposed method achieves higher structural anomaly detection accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Multiscale pattern learning for vibration-based structural anomaly detection: A benchmark dataset and validation study

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate simulation of streamflow in a catchment depends on selecting an appropriate model or model structure and equations that effectively represent the underlying hydrological processes. Further, model performance in a catchment is determined using performance metrics without explicit lower benchmarks. This study compares the effectiveness of conceptual lumped rainfall‐runoff (PB) and deep learning models compared to benchmark models across various catchment and climatic conditions for a benchmark‐informed, catchment‐attribute‐based model selection framework. Streamflow simulation was carried out using three PB models (GR4J, HBV, and SACSMA), as well as one deep learning model (LSTM). Model performance was assessed primarily using the Modified Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) metric and compared against catchment‐specific benchmark performance critical ranges derived from 17 benchmark models. In addition to modified KGE, four efficiency performance criteria such as high flow, low flow, water balance, and streamflow variability were evaluated to determine model robustness. A one‐dimensional analysis was conducted to explore how model efficiency varies with individual catchment characteristics. Additionally, a Classification and Regression Tree (CART) analysis was performed for each model to guide benchmark‐informed catchment‐specific model selection. The results suggest that PB models performed better in 70 catchments, achieving an average modified KGE of 0.82 in low aridity (< 0.7) and snow fraction (< 0.19), whereas the LSTM model was more effective in 82 catchments, achieving an average modified KGE of 0.68 in regions with a high snow fraction (> 0.22). The analysis offers significant understanding into the choice of models for streamflow simulation depending on catchment features/characteristics.

evidence_items.summary: Vancomycin has a narrow therapeutic window requiring individualized dosing and repeated monitoring, a process many health systems delegate from physicians to pharmacists. We silently deployed PharmaAgent, LLM-based vancomycin dosing agentic systems, at Stanford Hospital for two months and compared high- and low-autonomy configurations, each with and without institutional guidelines. Across 403 dosing events in 316 patients, mean absolute percentage error against the treating pharmacist's order was 21.8% with high autonomy versus 37.8% with low autonomy, and recommendations were within 25% of the order in 73.4% versus 50.9% of events (P < 0.001); a second pharmacist was within 25% of the treating pharmacist's order in 90.2% of events. Pharmacist review of 196 out-of-tolerance recommendations found a safety concern in 65.8%, more often with low autonomy (odds ratio 2.37). A higher-autonomy agent that self-debugged its steps proved more robust than stricter engineering, but neither configuration is ready to dose patients without pharmacist oversight.
evidence_items.title: PharmaAgent: a real-world evaluation of high- and low-autonomy agentic systems for inpatient vancomycin dosing

evidence_items.summary: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.
evidence_items.title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Concurrent faults in gears, bearings and shafts remain among the hardest cases for vibration-based condition monitoring of industrial gearboxes, because their signatures overlap, modulate one another and shift with speed and load. The 2009 PHM Society gearbox has become the standard public benchmark for this multi-component problem, yet published results on it are scattered across input types, network designs and validation schemes, which makes headline accuracies hard to compare. This article presents a critical review of deep-learning diagnosis on this benchmark and the wider gearbox literature, organised around three design choices: signal representation, model family and evaluation protocol. To ground the discussion, we re-analyse a controlled experiment in which three convolutional architectures were trained on 10,240 images per representation (continuous wavelet transform scalograms, short-time Fourier transform spectrograms and wavelet synchrosqueezed images) covering eight spur-gearbox health states. A compact five-stage batch-normalised network reached 99.90%, 99.85% and 99.66% test accuracy with wavelet, Synchrosqueezed and spectrogram inputs, respectively, but the margins among the best models correspond to only a few of the 2,048 test images. On a separate held-out validation subset, accuracy fell to 94.53%, 92.03% and 77.34%, making the representation effect far more visible. Comparison with published capsule-attention, architecture-search and transformer studies shows that reported accuracies on the same benchmark range from below 80% to above 99.5%, mainly because of differences in splitting protocol. We conclude with a reporting checklist and research agenda for leakage-aware, physics-informed and deployable gearbox diagnosis.
evidence_items.title: Deep Learning for Multi-Component Gearbox Fault Diagnosis on the PHM 2009 Benchmark: A Critical Review and Comparative Evaluation of Time–Frequency Representations and Network Architectures

evidence_items.summary: Background: Falls while carrying heavy loads on the head are an under-recognised mechanism of cervical spinal cord injury (CSCI) in Northern Nigeria. This study evaluated the clinical profile, outcomes, and predictors of good outcome in patients sustaining CSCI through this mechanism at a tertiary centre in Kano. Methods: A retrospective review of 16 male patients managed between January 2019 and June 2025 was conducted. Data on age, load weight, neurological level, completeness of injury, treatment modality, neurological improvement, and mortality were extracted. An aggregate outcome score was constructed from neurological improvement (yes = 1) and survival (alive = 1), with a total score of 2 defined as good outcome and 0–1 as poor outcome. Results: All patients were male (mean age 34.3 years). Loads ranged from 75–100 kg. C4 was the commonest level (8/16, 50%), followed by C5 (6/16, 37.5%). Ten patients (62.5%) had complete injuries and six (37.5%) incomplete injuries. Seven patients were managed conservatively and nine surgically. Among incomplete injuries, three improved by more than one neurological level and none died. Among complete injuries, three died. All deaths (3/9, 33.3%) occurred in the surgical group. Incomplete injury (p = 0.008) and conservative management (p = 0.015) were associated with good outcome. Conclusion: CSCI from head-loading falls predominantly affects young working-age males and carries a high mortality when the injury is complete. Incomplete injury and non-surgical management predicted good outcome. Preventive strategies targeting head-loading practices are urgently needed.
evidence_items.title: Cervical Spinal Cord Injury Due to Fall While Carrying Heavy Load on the Head in Kano, Nigeria: A Retrospective Analysis of Outcomes and Predictors of Good Outcome

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT. As urban areas transform into intelligent ecosystems, artificial intelligence technologies are assuming an increasingly vital role in the prevention of urban crime. This research amalgamates artificial intelligence with conventional criminological theories, specifically Routine Activity Theory (RAT) and Crime Pattern Theory (CPT) to theorize framework and practical approaches to urban crime prevention. To methodically evaluate the convergence of artificial intelligence implementation in urban crime deterrence. AI implements predictive policing and real-time monitoring, establishing a novel kind of oversight that perpetually observes metropolitan environments, hence diminishing prospects for criminal activity. This study contends that multidisciplinary methodologies for urban crime prevention, integrating technology with social and spatial theories, yield more successful and nuanced solutions. The findings convey a definitive message: although technology and urban design are significant, the primary emphasis for effective crime prevention is in education, preventive measures, and the strategic integration of digital tools.

evidence_items.summary: Publisher contracts usually contain many specific clauses around open access publishing and full text access. But what is said about (open) metadata in these contracts, and how does this differ across publishers and consortia? To get a better overview on this, it is useful to systematically collect information on how metadata are currently included in publisher contracts. This information can provide examples of current practice, including differences among how publishers and consortia approach this topic. Looking forward, this can inform future negotiations around open metadata in publisher contracts. The ESAC Registry of Open Publishing Agreements, maintained by OA2020, provided access to a large corpus of publisher contracts, many of which are available in full text. This allows for a systematic analysis of the extent to which open metadata are currently included in such contracts, and for the resulting data to be publicly shared. As of December 2025, the ESAC registry contained 635 current contracts (i.e. valid in 2025), of which 230 included a link to the full text of the contract. In total, full text contracts are available for 23 countries (or groups of countries) and 48 publishers. Initially, we looked at contracts from two library consortia, Jisc (UK) and Bibsam (Sweden) as well as publisher contracts across Germany (DEAL, TIB and SUB Göttingen).
evidence_items.title: Your contract says 'Open Access', but does it say 'Open Metadata'?

evidence_items.summary: A new PID is born. In this session, you will discover how the Open Registry for Awards and Prizes (ORAP) helps you bring structure to fragmented award information and turn scattered data into something reusable, linkable, and genuinely useful. If you have ever tried to track prizes awarded across departments, databases, or spreadsheets, you already know how messy this landscape can be. ORAP aims to fix exactly that. We will start with a practical introduction to the registry, which officially launched in February 2026 with more than 1,900 curated awards and a metadata model consisting of 22 fields. Each award receives a unique ORAP-PRIZE-ID, giving it a stable and citable identity. Where possible, ORAP also connects awards to external knowledge sources such as Wikidata, and future extensions will include linking awarding organizations through ROR IDs to make the ecosystem even more interoperable. In a short live demo, you experience how ORAP can be used to explore and filter award data, support institutional reporting and enable new use cases in research information management. You will get insight into how the metadata schema is designed—what is included, what is not, and which fields are essential for describing awards in a consistent, machine readable way. Beyond the technical foundation, we’ll show how ORAP grows through a community-driven curation process. You learn how new awards are submitted, reviewed, improved, and finally integrated into the registry, and why community stewardship is crucial for keeping the dataset accurate, transparent, and up to date. This session is especially relevant if you work with research information systems, persistent identifiers or metadata standards and want to understand how prize data can be structured and integrated into the PID ecosystem. If you are curious how a new identifier system comes to life—and how you can contribute—this is your chance.
evidence_items.title: Lessons Learned from ORAP: Structuring Prizes with PIDs in Practice

evidence_items.summary: As data volumes and complexity grow the question of how to scale Persistent Identifier (PID) systems becomes increasingly important. In practice, data is often organized in hierarchies - from collections to datasets to individual files - raising a key challenge: Which level of detail truly benefits users whilst keeping the systems operational? This session invites participants to share real-world use cases, challenges, and approaches to PID assignment across different domains. Depending on the context, PIDs at the collection or publication level may be sufficient for discovery and citation, while more granular identifiers are required for reproducibility, automated workflows, and machine actionability. However, increased granularity  introduces overhead and complexity, potentially leading to unsustainable proliferation of identifiers. We aim to bring together diverse perspectives from different stakeholders to explore how decisions about PID granularity are made in practice, and how to balance the trade-off between too many and too few PIDs.
evidence_items.title: What Deserves a PID? Scalability, Scope and Granularity in Real-World PID Use Cases

evidence_items.summary: Description This dataset provides an integrated, non-redundant collection of 3,942,958 viral-associated protein sequences designed to facilitate preliminary homology-based screening and prioritization of candidate viral contigs in large-scale metagenomic assemblies. The database was constructed using viral-associated protein annotations from CheckV v1.5 as the primary selection criteria. Protein sequences were collected from multiple public resources, including Pfam-A, Pfam-B, VOGDB, KEGG, IMG/VR, RVDB, NCBI RefSeq viruses, and CheckV representative protein sequences. For resources with directly retrievable protein sequences, corresponding proteins were extracted using CheckV-associated identifiers. For other sequence resources, viral-associated protein profiles were searched against protein datasets using HMMER, followed by filtering based on CheckV HMM-specific score cutoffs. All collected protein sequences were merged and assigned source-specific identifiers. Redundant sequences were subsequently clustered using MMseqs2 with a minimum sequence identity of 90% (--min-seq-id 0.9), a minimum target coverage of 80% (-c 0.8), the greedy incremental clustering algorithm (--cluster-mode 2), and the target coverage mode (--cov-mode 1). The resulting non-redundant collection contains 3,942,958 unique protein sequence identifiers , comprising a total of 1,053,174,911 amino acids . Usage example A typical workflow involves predicting protein-coding genes from assembled contigs, searching the predicted proteins against the reference database using DIAMOND BLASTP, and selecting contigs with one or more qualifying protein matches for further analysis. 1. Build a DIAMOND database. diamond makedb --in viruses.nr rep seq.fasta.gz --db viruses.nr rep seq 2. Predict proteins from metagenomic contigs. prodigal -i contigs.fna -a contigs.faa -p meta 3. Search predicted proteins against the database.
evidence_items.title: An integrated non-redundant viral-associated protein reference database for metagenomic sequence screening

evidence_items.summary: The Personal AI Constitution, Version 2.0, establishes a human-governed framework for the responsible integration of artificial intelligence into research, STEM education, creative production, and international development. Developed by Professor Moustapha Diack within the Human–AI Research Partnerships (HARP-AI) initiative, the Constitution articulates sixteen foundational principles addressing human authority, cognitive augmentation, critical thinking, verification, transparency, justice, equity, diversity, inclusion (JEDI), cultural sovereignty, synthetic identities, intellectual property, creative labor, and responsible commercialization. The Constitution affirms that human researchers and creators retain final responsibility for scholarly integrity, ethical judgment, cultural interpretation, intellectual independence, and creative decisions. It also establishes principles for evaluating AI research partnerships and maintaining human oversight of AI-assisted activities. Particular attention is given to historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs), Senegal, Francophone Africa, and AI for Development (AI4D). BAMBUGARE AI Music Studio provides a context for examining cultural memory, synthetic artistic identities, creative provenance, and economic justice. Approved on October 31, 2026, Version 2.0 serves as the foundational governance framework for the HARP-AI research program. It is a personal scholarly governance document and does not imply institutional endorsement by Southern University or endorsement by AI technology providers.
evidence_items.title: Professor Diack - Personal AI Constitution: Human-Governed Intelligence, Justice, Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion

evidence_items.summary: Revumenib (formerly SNDX-5613) is a novel, potent and oral menin inhibitor employed in clinical settings because of treating acute myeloid leukemia in critically ill patients.  Nevertheless, safety is still a matter of concern due to the optimal timing of administration and  doses of this anticancer agent. An effective tool that allows to solve the drug dosage regimen is  therapeutic drug monitoring. In that sense, simple, sensitive and accurate bioanalytical strategies  are required. Here, a rapid capillary electrophoresis with diode-array detector methodology was  developed and applied for the first time to detect, identify and determine revumenib in complex  clinical matrices such as human blood serum in less than 5 minutes of analysis with a minimal  sample preparation procedure based on a protein precipitation with acetonitrile. Various chemical  and instrumental critical parameters were rigorously optimized for the separation process in a  fused-silica capillary with a background electrolyte of phosphate buffer (50 mM, pH=2.0) in  deionized water. Adequate analytical performance parameters were obtained involving a good  linearity, detection and quantification limits at ng mL⁻¹ levels, and a correct precision and  accuracy. Furthermore, this approach can be characterized as an ecofriendly strategy in the  bioanalysis field based on an estimated greenness evaluation via AGREEprep and AGREE metrics tool  with acceptable scores. Considering the results, the present work can be used as a new medical tool  and successfully applied in the therapeutic monitoring of revumenib in routine clinical  laboratories but also to take appropriate decisions in future (pre)clinical trials and/or phases.
evidence_items.title: A rapid and green analytical strategy to determine menin inhibitor revumenib in human blood serum via CE-DAD

evidence_items.summary: This conceptual working paper introduces HARP-AI (Human–AI Research Partnerships), a human-governed framework for integrating artificial intelligence into scholarly research, education, creative production, and AI for Development (AI4D). Grounded in the Personal AI Constitution developed by Professor Moustapha Diack, the framework establishes human authority, critical thinking, verification, transparency, justice, equity, diversity, inclusion, cultural sovereignty, and creative economic justice as governing principles for human–AI collaboration. The paper distinguishes AI research collaborators from creative production tools, distribution platforms, and research documentation instruments. It proposes a governance and evaluation framework for assessing AI systems while maintaining nondelegable human responsibility for research integrity, ethical judgment, cultural representation, and scholarly publication. BAMBUGARE AI Music Studio serves as an illustrative case of AI-assisted cultural production linking Senegalese and Louisiana musical heritage. The discussion examines fictional virtual artists, memorial naming, synthetic identity, creative provenance, intellectual property, and equitable cultural participation. The paper also outlines a prospective research agenda for investigating the educational, cultural, and developmental implications of human-governed AI ecosystems, particularly in historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs), Senegal, and Francophone Africa. As a conceptual contribution, the paper does not claim empirical validation of the proposed framework. It offers a foundation for future research, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible AI4D practice.
evidence_items.title: Constituting Human–AI Research Partnerships: A Human-Governed AI4D Framework for Constitutional Governance, Cultural Sovereignty, and Creative Justice

evidence_items.summary: The educational component of the study aims to evaluate the impact of students' active involvement in the design, programming, implementation, and experimental validation of a robotic sorting system on the development of computational thinking, technical skills, and collaborative competencies. The educational outcomes are assessed using two complementary evaluation instruments. The development of computational thinking and technical skills is objectively measured by comparing students' performance in pre-test and post-test assessments, whereas students' perceptions of teamwork, consensus building, and active engagement in the learning process are investigated through a post-study questionnaire administered after the experimental activities. This combined evaluation approach provides a comprehensive assessment of both measurable learning outcomes and students' perceived educational experiences and directly addresses Research Questions RQ5 and RQ6.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Seed implant brachytherapy (SIBT) is an effective cancer treatment modality; however, clinical planning often relies on manual adjustment of objective function weights, leading to inefficiencies and suboptimal results. This study proposes an adaptive weight optimization framework for SIBT planning, driven by large language models (LLMs). A locally deployed DeepSeek‐R1 LLM is integrated with an automatic planning algorithm in an iterative loop. Starting with fixed weights, the LLM evaluates plan quality and recommends new weights in the next iteration. This process continues until convergence criteria are met, after which the LLM conducts a comprehensive evaluation to identify the optimal plan. A clinical knowledge base, constructed and queried via retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG), enhances the model's domain‐specific reasoning. The proposed method was retrospectively validated on 23 patient cases who underwent head‐and‐neck SIBT, showing that the LLM‐assisted approach maintained clinical target volume (CTV) coverage and reduced excessive target dose relative to fixed‐weight planning; in the eight patients with available organs at risk (OARs) contours, OAR dose metrics showed favorable numerical trends. The study demonstrates the potential of LLMs as assistive tools for SIBT planning under clinician supervision.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model Framework for Seed Implant Brachytherapy: Adaptive Weight Optimization via Retrieval‐Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO₂ emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO₂ emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: CAISO, ERCOT, MISO, and PJM. Using Meta's LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours. In PJM, where subregional MOER profiles are largely homogeneous, spatial flexibility achieves only 0.3% emissions reduction while temporal flexibility reaches up to 17.2% lesser emissions than S1.
evidence_items.title: Carbon-aware scheduling of Large Language Model training across multiple US power grid operators: a marginal emissions analysis

evidence_items.summary: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.
evidence_items.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
